items.title: Pakistan’s natural resources worth $8-10tr at 'most conservative estimate', says Dar
items.description: Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar on Friday said that the estimated worth of minerals, hydrocarbons and other natural resources in Pakistan was between $8 trillion and $10tr. And this was the “most conservative estimate”, he said while addressing a ceremony held in Karachi to mark the arrival of a Turkish seismic research vessel, Oruc Reis. The vessel, which arrived on Thursday, will be used for offshore oil and gas exploration in Pakistan. Dar began his address by welcoming the leadership and professionals of the Turkish Petroleum, as well as the captain, crew and seismic research team of Oruc Reis, and termed the occasion a “historic moment”. He noted that Oruc Reis brought “Turkish scientific expertise together with the experience and capabilities of our national energy companies to advance exploration in Pakistan’s offshore domain”. Dar added, “Every successful journey of exploration begins with knowledge. The data gathered by this vessel may deepen our understanding of the geological structures beneath the seabed and provide a stronger basis for Pakistan’s future exploration plan.” He described offshore exploration as “complex, capital-intensive and inherently uncertain”. And a seismic survey could not guarantee a commercial discovery, he continued. “But no discovery can be made without seismic and exploration,” he stressed, adding that today, Pakistan was taking that step with “confidence, responsibility and the prayers of our people”. He said Pakistan sought a long-term energy partnership with Turkiye, encompassing offshore exploration, minerals and renewable energy. “You all have witnessed three memorandums of understanding signed between the relevant Turkish and Pakistani agencies. “We want Pakistani geologists and engineers to work very closely with their Turkish counterparts. We want our universities and research institutions to develop partnerships in marine, geoscience and offshore engineering,” he said. He assured “our Turkish partners and brothers” that the government of Pakistan would extend every appropriate facilitation to the “very important mission” to be undertaken by Oruc Reis. “All offshore activities must observe the highest standards of maritime safety and environmental protection. Our seas are an economic asset, but they are also a national trust. Development and environmental stewardship must proceed together,” he stressed. Dar further said that the Turkish energy minister told him that the seismic mission would take around five to six months. “I said, you won’t be allowed to leave unless you give us good news of a real discovery,” he added. He said he would come across people who described Pakistan as a country in a debt trap. He went on to say the estimated value of the country’s natural resources, including mines and minerals, hydrocarbons, gemstones and rare earth materials, far exceeded its debt burden. “Sometimes people talk about Pakistan being in debt, being a heavily indebted country, or being in a debt-trap; I always negate that,” he said, adding that Pakistan was endowed with abundant natural resources. He thanked the Turkish government and people for standing alongside Pakistan and described the arrival of the Oruc Reis as another example of the two countries’ partnership. The arrival of the Oruç Reis vessel follows the government’s revival of offshore exploration efforts after a gap of nearly two decades. The Offshore Bid Round 2025 was launched in January last year, offering 40 offshore blocks in the Indus and Makran basins for petroleum exploration. Turkish Petroleum Offshore Company (TPOC), a subsidiary of Turkish Petroleum Corporation, has partnered with local state-owned energy companies, including Oil and Gas Development Company Limited (OGDCL), Mari Energies and Pakistan Petroleum Limited (PPL), for exploration activities in three blocks. It holds a 25 per cent interest and operatorship in the Eastern Offshore Indus-C block in the Arabian Sea, alongside stakes in two onshore blocks. Pakistan’s offshore zone covers around 300,000 square kilometres, but only 18 wells have been drilled there since independence in 1947. A basin study by US firm DeGolyer and MacNaughton has identified significant untapped hydrocarbon potential in the country’s offshore basins.

items.title: JPMorgan, Visa, Mastercard : les données de milliers de clients exposées, l'IA amplifie la menace cyber
items.description: Nouvelle faille dans la protection des donnees bancaires. Le 19 novembre, JPMorgan Chase, Visa et Mastercard ont reconnu des cyberattaques visant des prestataires exterieurs, exposant des informations sur certains clients. Leurs reseaux de paiement n'ont pas ete compromis, assurent les entreprises. Chez JPMorgan, les pirates auraient accede a des fichiers marketing contenant noms et adresses electroniques. Reuters a examine des donnees presentees comme celles de plus de 16 000 clients, parfois accompagnees de numeros de telephone, sans pouvoir les authentifier. Mastercard evoque un nombre limite d'adresses de courriel d'adherents a un programme d'avantages. Visa signale un incident chez un fournisseur en Asie-Pacifique, sans atteinte a ses systemes ni aux numeros de cartes. L'intelligence artificielle de tous les dangers Les entreprises n'ont pas identifie leurs prestataires. Le groupe d'extorsion n0n a revendique les attaques et publie des echantillons de fichiers, dont la provenance reste a verifier. La panne ayant perturbe JPMorgan le 16 novembre relevait, elle, d'un bug logiciel distinct. Au-dela des donnees derobees, l'affaire revele une faiblesse structurelle : une banque peut securiser son propre reseau tout en restant exposee par ses sous-traitants. Une adresse electronique associee a un etablissement financier suffit parfois a preparer des messages frauduleux credibles. L'intelligence artificielle (IA) accentue la menace. Selon le specialiste de cybersecurite SOCRadar, n0n a utilise un assistant de programmation fonde sur l'IA pour developper des centaines de scripts d'attaque. Le constat concerne les methodes documentees du groupe, sans etablir le role de l'IA dans les intrusions precises. Les outils d'IA accelerent la preparation des attaques et facilitent les campagnes d'hameconnage personnalisees a grande echelle. Le defi n'est donc plus seulement de proteger les banques, mais de securiser toute la chaîne de prestataires auxquels elles confient leurs donnees.

items.title: Before we liberalise, we must learn to produce
items.description: Walk into one of Ghana’s growing China Malls and the economic reality confronting the country becomes difficult to ignore. The shelves are full. The prices are attractive. Consumers have access to household items, electronics, furniture, clothing, tools and countless other products at prices many local retailers struggle to match. From the perspective of the ghanaian consumer, this is good news. But from the perspective of an economy trying to industrialise, there is a much bigger question: What happens to a country when it becomes exceptionally good at consuming what other countries are exceptionally good at producing? This is the question Ghana must confront. China Malls are not necessarily the cause of Ghana’s industrial weakness. They are, rather, a visible symptom of a deeper structural problem: Ghana has liberalised consumption faster than it has built productive capacity. China’s position in Ghana’s import economy illustrates the scale of the challenge. Ghana Statistical Service data show that China remained Ghana’s largest import partner in 2024, with imports from China rising from GHS 33.9 billion in 2023 to GHS 56.8 billion in 2024.¹ WTO data similarly place China among the largest single sources of Ghana’s merchandise imports.² So the question should not simply be whether Ghanaians should patronise China Mall. The deeper question is: Why are we importing so much of what we could eventually produce ourselves? The China Mall Is Not the Enemy We must be careful here. China has become extraordinarily competitive because it built an industrial ecosystem capable of producing at scale, cheaply and increasingly technologically. Chinese firms have factories, logistics networks, financing mechanisms, supply chains and access to enormous domestic and international markets. That is precisely the lesson Ghana should be learning. Recent research on Chinese private capital in Ghana shows that the Chinese commercial presence is evolving beyond simply importing finished products. Some Chinese businesses are increasingly assembling and manufacturing in Ghana, while Chinese-linked manufacturing operations have begun supplying products to local markets and, in some cases, the wider African market. That is potentially positive. If a Chinese company establishes a factory in Ghana, employs Ghanaians, transfers technology, sources inputs locally, develops Ghanaian suppliers and exports through AfCFTA, then Ghana is not simply importing China. Ghana is capturing part of China’s productive capacity. That is the model we should pursue. The problem arises when our economic relationship with the rest of the world is overwhelmingly organised around importing finished goods and exporting raw materials. That is not strategic autonomy. It is commercial dependency. The Problem With Liberalising Before Industrialising For decades, developing countries have often been told that free trade will produce efficiency. There is truth in that argument. Competition can force companies to become more productive. Imports can give consumers cheaper goods. Foreign investment can bring technology and capital. Access to international markets can create opportunities for exporters. But there is an important question that conventional free-trade arguments sometimes overlook: competition between whom? A Ghanaian manufacturer with expensive electricity, expensive credit, limited access to technology, high logistics costs, and a relatively small domestic market is not necessarily competing on equal terms with a Chinese manufacturer operating inside one of the world’s largest industrial ecosystems. Opening the market does not magically create equality between the two. It can instead eliminate the Ghanaian producer before that producer has had the opportunity to become competitive. This is the fundamental logic behind the infant-industry argument. An infant industry cannot necessarily compete with an established foreign industry on day one. It needs time, capital, technology, infrastructure, skilled workers, and access to markets — and, sometimes, temporary protection. The argument is not that Ghanaian companies should be protected forever. It is that you cannot expect a seedling to compete with a fully grown tree simply because both have been placed in the same forest. Britain Did Not Become Powerful by Preaching Free Trade From the Beginning There is an uncomfortable historical reality about the contemporary free-trade debate: some of the countries that eventually became the strongest advocates of open markets did not industrialize under completely open markets. Britain is perhaps the most important example. For centuries, British commercial policy contained strong protectionist and mercantilist elements. The Navigation Acts, beginning in the seventeenth century, sought to control shipping and commercial flows in favour of English interests. The Corn Laws later protected British agriculture through restrictions and tariffs on imported grain.⁴ Britain eventually became a powerful advocate of free trade, particularly after the repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 and the Navigation Acts in 1849. The lesson is not that protectionism automatically creates prosperity. It is that trade policy has historically been connected to the stage of economic development and national strategy. Britain liberalised from a position of considerable industrial strength. That distinction matters for Ghana. We should not confuse the economic policy appropriate for an industrial power with the policy appropriate for a country still trying to build an industrial base. America Understood the Infant-Industry Argument The United States provides another important case. Alexander Hamilton’s Report on Manufactures, submitted to Congress in 1791, argued for the deliberate development of American manufacturing and included protective tariffs as part of that strategy.⁵ The early American industrial-policy framework explicitly recognised tariffs as a means of nurturing infant industries, and the United States subsequently developed a long tradition of tariff protection, particularly through the nineteenth century. This history should not be romanticised. Protectionism has also produced failures: the Smoot-Hawley tariffs of 1930 became associated with a destructive period of trade retaliation and contributed to the deterioration of international trade during the Great Depression.⁶ That is precisely why Ghana should not pursue blind protectionism. The lesson is not “tariffs are always good.” The lesson is that trade policy must serve industrial strategy. South Korea Provides Perhaps the More Relevant Lesson For Ghana, South Korea may be an even more useful comparison. South Korea emerged from war with very limited industrial capacity. Yet it did not simply wait for the market to determine what the country should produce. The Korean state actively directed credit, protected selected industries, promoted exports and supported strategic sectors. During the 1970s, South Korea aggressively pursued heavy and chemical industrialisation. Research on the country’s Heavy and Chemical Industry Drive finds that these policies expanded targeted industries and generated benefits that persisted even after the policies themselves ended.⁷ South Korea subsequently became more open as its industrial capacity strengthened. Ghana’s Problem Is Not Simply Imports. It Is the Structure of Our Economy. Ghana cannot realistically produce everything. Nor should it. No serious economic strategy would require Ghana to manufacture every smartphone, aircraft, computer chip, or medical machine consumed domestically. Strategic autonomy does not mean autarky — it means having enough domestic productive capacity that the country is not structurally vulnerable. The objective should therefore be selective. Ghana should identify strategic sectors where domestic production is economically and technologically feasible, and where excessive import dependence creates economic vulnerability. These could include: Agro-processing Pharmaceuticals Textiles and garments Furniture Building materials Basic chemicals Machinery and agricultural equipment Packaging Food processing Selected electronics assembly Renewable-energy components Defence and security-related production Digital and technology services The objective should be value addition. Why should Ghana export cocoa and import chocolate? Why should we export minerals and import finished products containing those minerals? Why should we produce cotton and agricultural raw materials but import the finished consumer goods that could instead create manufacturing jobs here? Why should the Ghanaian market become the final destination for other people’s industrial production? The China Model Itself Offers Ghana an Important Lesson Ironically, perhaps the greatest lesson China offers Ghana is not to import Chinese goods. It is how China built the capacity to produce them. China’s economic rise was built around manufacturing, infrastructure, industrial clusters, export capacity, technological learning and massive investment in productive capabilities. Today, China continues to prioritise advanced manufacturing as a central pillar of its economic strategy — and Western governments increasingly complain about Chinese industrial overcapacity precisely because China’s producer-oriented economic model keeps generating enormous manufacturing capacity and export competitiveness. Ghana should therefore look at the China Mall and ask a different question. Not “how do we stop Chinese products?” but “how do we develop Ghanaian firms capable of competing with them?” That is a far more strategic question. Protectionism Must Come With Discipline There is a major danger here. If Ghana protects domestic businesses without demanding performance, protectionism will simply create comfortable monopolies. That would be disastrous. A Ghanaian company should not receive protection merely because it is Ghanaian. Protection should be conditional: if government gives a company tariff protection, that company should carry measurable obligations in return. For example: Years 1–3: increase domestic production and employment. Years 3–5: increase local sourcing and technological capability. Years 5–7: meet specified productivity and quality standards. Years 7–10: demonstrate export competitiveness. Failure to meet agreed targets should trigger the withdrawal of protection. This transforms protectionism from a political favour into an industrial contract between the state and the private sector. We Should Also Distinguish Between Inputs and Finished Products This is critical. Ghana should not impose indiscriminate tariffs on everything. If a Ghanaian furniture manufacturer imports machinery, specialised components or production inputs that cannot yet be produced domestically, heavily taxing those imports may actually hurt industrialization. Instead, the tariff structure should distinguish between productive inputs and finished consumer goods. Importing a machine that allows a Ghanaian factory to produce 100,000 units is economically different from importing 100,000 finished units that compete directly with that factory. Industrial policy must make it cheaper to produce than simply to import and resell. Ghana Should Use AfCFTA as the Exit Strategy This is where protectionism connects directly with the broader argument about Ghana’s strategic autonomy. Strategic autonomy does not mean Ghana withdrawing from the world. It means Ghana becoming strong enough to engage the world on better terms. The principle remains: Work with everybody, but become dependent on nobody. The economic version of that principle should be: Build for Ghana → Scale for Africa → Compete globally The Ghanaian market is too small to be the final destination of an ambitious industrial strategy. But Ghana can use its domestic market as the training ground for African companies. A Ghanaian pharmaceutical company should first become competitive in Ghana, then expand into Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire, Senegal, Kenya and the wider African market. A Ghanaian clothing manufacturer should not think of 34 million Ghanaians as its entire market; it should think of the African Continental Free Trade Area as its eventual market. The World Bank has argued that deeper AfCFTA integration could substantially increase Ghana’s trade with African partners and create opportunities for greater value-added exports.⁸ Protectionism, therefore, should not be an alternative to AfCFTA. It should be used to prepare Ghanaian firms to take advantage of it. China Should Be a Partner in Ghana’s Industrialisation — Not Merely a Supplier to Ghanaian Consumers There is also a diplomatic dimension. Ghana does not need to choose between China and the West that would be the wrong strategic framework. Ghana needs China: Chinese capital, technology, machinery, industrial expertise, and access to Chinese markets. But we must negotiate from the position of a country that knows what it wants. Instead of: China produces → Ghana imports → Ghana consumes We should be pursuing: China invests and transfers technology → Ghana produces → Ghana adds value → Ghana exports to Africa That is a fundamentally different relationship, and it is consistent with strategic autonomy. Foreign direct investment should increasingly be judged not simply by how much capital enters Ghana, but by what productive capability remains after the investor arrives: how many Ghanaian workers are trained, how many Ghanaian suppliers are developed, how much technology is transferred, how much local value is created, how much is exported, and how much of the supply chain becomes Ghanaian. These are the questions that should define investment diplomacy. The Ghanaian Consumer Cannot Be Blamed It is easy to tell Ghanaians to “buy made in Ghana.” But that slogan is insufficient. A worker earning a modest salary will naturally choose the product that costs GHS 100 rather than the one costing GHS 160. We cannot moralise consumer behaviour while ignoring production economics. If we want Ghanaians to buy Ghanaian products, those products must become affordable, reliable, attractive and competitive. The responsibility falls primarily on policymakers and producers: government must create the environment, businesses must improve productivity, banks must finance production, universities must produce industrial skills, and technical institutions must support manufacturing. Consumers will then reward competitive local products — not before. The Real Danger Is Not China Mall The real danger is becoming permanently comfortable as a consuming economy. There is nothing inherently wrong with a Chinese shop selling a Ghanaian consumer an affordable product. But if thousands of such shops can expand while thousands of potential Ghanaian factories never emerge, then something is fundamentally wrong with our economic architecture. The question is not whether China Mall should exist. The question is whether Ghana Mall, Ghanaian factories, Ghanaian supply chains and Ghanaian brands can emerge alongside it and eventually compete with it. That is the real test. We Should Not Liberalise Because Economists Tell Us To; We Should Liberalise When Our Producers Are Ready This is the central argument. Ghana should not embrace protectionism as an ideology any more than it should embrace free trade as an ideology. Both are instruments. The question is what Ghana needs at this stage of its development. For a country whose merchandise exports remain heavily concentrated in commodities, and whose participation in global value chains is still limited, the priority must be building productive capacity and increasing domestic value addition. The World Bank has itself noted Ghana’s continued dependence on a small number of primary commodities and the need to deepen manufacturing participation in global value chains.⁹ Ghana should therefore consider a long-term, strategic and conditional protectionist industrial policy. Not protection forever. Not closed borders. Not hostility towards foreign investors. Not isolation. But a deliberate period in which the Ghanaian state says: we will give Ghanaian production the space to grow. We will protect strategic industries where necessary. We will make production cheaper. We will make importing finished goods relatively less attractive than importing productive inputs. We will demand performance from protected firms. We will invest in energy, transport, skills, technology and finance. We will use government procurement to create markets for competitive Ghanaian firms. We will attract foreign investors who bring technology and productive capacity. And when Ghanaian companies become sufficiently competitive, we will expose them to greater international competition. That is how protection becomes a bridge rather than a prison. From Political Sovereignty to Economic Sovereignty Ghana achieved political independence in 1957. But political independence without productive capacity has limits. A country that cannot manufacture basic goods, process its raw materials, develop technology, finance its businesses, or feed its population independently remains vulnerable to external economic pressures. This is why the debate about China Malls is ultimately bigger than China Malls. It is about the kind of economy Ghana wants to become. Strategic autonomy should not merely mean having a flag, a government, and diplomatic recognition. It requires the internal capacity to make meaningful choices — and that principle applies directly to trade. We cannot claim strategic autonomy while importing the foundations of our everyday economic life. The objective is therefore not to shut Ghana off from the world. It is to build a Ghana capable of negotiating with the world. We should trade with China, with Europe, with America, with India, with our African neighbors. But we must also build factories, supply chains, technology, capital, skills, Ghanaian brands, African markets and eventually, companies that can walk into the same markets from which today’s imports are arriving, and compete. That is the difference between participating in globalisation and simply being consumed by it. Ghana does not need permanent protection. Ghana needs enough time and policy discipline to learn how to produce before it is asked to compete with those who already know how to produce at scale. The ultimate objective should be simple: Protect Ghanaian production. Build Ghanaian capacity. Scale through Africa. Then compete with the world. That is not isolation. That is strategic autonomy. Author : Amin Mohammed is a Ghanaian development communication practitioner, author, and entrepreneur with interests in leadership, innovation, international relations, and Africa’s economic transformation.

items.title: 2030: FG takes decisive action to end open defecation with Executive Order
items.description: By Gabriel Ewepu ABUJA – IN a renewed commitment, the Federal Government has unveiled a new Executive Order to accelerate Nigeria’s drive towards ending open defecation by 2030. The unveiling of the Open Defecation Free Nigeria by 2030 and Other Related Matters Order, 2025 coincided with the commemoration of World Toilet Day and the seventh anniversary of the Clean Nigeria campaign in Abuja on Thursday. Vice President Kashim Shettima, represented by the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Delivery and Coordination in the Office of the Vice President, Akubo Adegbe, described the Executive Order as a decisive step towards translating government commitments into measurable sanitation outcomes. Shettima said the order marks a transition from fragmented interventions to stronger coordination, measurable results and sustainable national progress. He called on state and local governments to strengthen accountability, increase sanitation financing and sustain community-led behavioural change He disclosed that since the launch of the Clean Nigeria campaign in 2019, 185 of the country’s 774 local government areas have attained Open Defecation Free (ODF) status, while Jigawa and Katsina remain the only states certified as ODF nationwide. While acknowledging the progress recorded, the Vice President warned that the country still had considerable ground to cover, urging states yet to achieve ODF status to establish monthly and quarterly targets and make their progress publicly available. He also cautioned against a reversal of gains in communities already certified as open defecation-free, stressing the need for sustained monitoring and accountability to protect existing achievements. According to him, Nigeria must prioritise sustainable financing, reliable data, stronger institutions, effective implementation and continuous behavioural change to achieve the 2030 target. He also called on state and local governments to take ownership of the campaign by allocating adequate resources and strengthening sanitation institutions, while urging development partners, the private sector, traditional rulers, community leaders and civil society organisations to sustain their support. Shettima, who chairs the Steering Committee of the Clean Nigeria Project, reaffirmed the Federal Government’s commitment to working with subnational governments, noting that the National Economic Council would also be deployed to advance and sustain the national sanitation agenda. Linking the campaign to this year’s World Toilet Day theme, “Sanitation and Gender Equality,” the Vice President highlighted the disproportionate burden poor sanitation places on women and girls. He noted that inadequate access to safe and private sanitation facilities undermines their health, security, dignity, education and participation in economic and social activities. He called for inclusive policies and investments that address the sanitation needs of women, girls, persons with disabilities and other vulnerable populations. Meanwhile, the Minister of Water Resources and Sanitation, Engr Joseph Utsev, in his speech said the Clean Nigeria campaign had evolved beyond public awareness and mobilisation into a national platform for policy coordination, institutional engagement, community participation and performance monitoring. Utsev highlighted the revised Clean Nigeria Strategy 2025–2030, which is structured around six strategic pillars, as well as the newly introduced Clean Nigeria Real Time Monitoring and Information System designed to improve data management, track implementation and strengthen accountability. Reflecting on the campaign’s seven-year journey, the minister identified five critical lessons, including the need to translate political commitment into adequate financing and practical action, prevent communities from relapsing into open defecation, strengthen community ownership, adopt a multi-sectoral approach and ensure that reliable data informs planning and resource allocation. The Minister of Youth Development, Ayodele Olawande, said the ministry was contributing to the campaign through youth mobilisation and community advocacy, disclosing that more than 1,000 youth volunteers had been trained to promote sanitation awareness and behavioural change. He said pilot interventions were ongoing in Bauchi, Kaduna, Benue, Ebonyi and Oyo states, adding that young people also had an important role to play in promoting gender-responsive sanitation. Olawande specifically emphasised menstrual hygiene education, access to safe and private toilet facilities and the need to eliminate the stigma associated with menstruation. Goodwill messages were also delivered by the former Head of the Civil Service of the Federation, Didi Esther Walson-Jack, alongside representatives of civil society organisations, professional bodies and development partners, who reaffirmed the importance of collective action in achieving Nigeria’s 2030 open defecation elimination target. items.title: Élections en Espagne : pourquoi une victoire de la droite ne devrait pas inquiéter Rabat
items.description: À l’approche des élections législatives espagnoles, prévues le 29 novembre 2026, les enjeux dépassent les frontières de l’Espagne. Pour le Maroc, dont les relations avec son voisin du nord ont connu plusieurs évolutions ces dernières années, l’issue du scrutin revêt une importance particulière, notamment au regard des positions des différentes formations politiques espagnoles sur les relations bilatérales. L’Espagne entame la première semaine de sa campagne électorale dans un contexte politique ouvert à plusieurs scénarios. Malgré l’avance du Parti populaire (PP), de droite conservatrice, dans plusieurs sondages d’opinion, certaines projections lui attribuent la possibilité d’obtenir, avec le soutien de Vox, formation d’extrême droite, une majorité absolue au Parlement. Toutefois, l’issue du scrutin ne dépend pas uniquement des rapports de force mesurés dans les enquêtes d’opinion, mais également de la capacité des partis en lice à nouer des alliances pour former le prochain gouvernement. Pour Abdelhamid Benkhattab, professeur de sciences politiques à la faculté de droit Agdal-Rabat, une éventuelle victoire de la droite espagnole ne devrait toutefois pas entraîner de détérioration substantielle des relations entre Rabat et Madrid. Dans une analyse livrée à Hespress FR , l’universitaire estime que les formations politiques situées aux extrêmes de l’échiquier espagnol ne disposent pas nécessairement des moyens d’infléchir durablement la politique étrangère du pays. « Nous avons déjà l’expérience que les partis minoritaires d’extrême gauche ou d’extrême droite ne déterminent pas définitivement la politique espagnole à l’égard du Maroc. Ils ne détériorent pas nécessairement non plus les relations maroco-espagnoles », souligne-t-il, en référence notamment aux positions de Sumar et de Podemos, dont les prises de position sur le Maroc n’ont pas, selon lui, véritablement pesé sur la politique étrangère espagnole. Dans cette perspective, même une entrée de Vox au gouvernement ne constituerait pas, à ses yeux, un facteur déterminant dans l’évolution des relations bilatérales. Benkhattab considère que le Parti populaire, malgré certaines prises de position critiques à l’égard du Maroc au cours de la campagne, reste avant tout une formation de gouvernement, dotée d’une culture pragmatique. L’universitaire estime ainsi que le Parti populaire (PP) ne devrait pas nécessairement suivre Vox dans ses positions les plus hostiles à l’égard de Rabat. Il interprète plutôt les déclarations et les prises de position du parti conservateur comme relevant d'une stratégie électorale destinée à séduire une partie de l’électorat situé à l’extrême droite et à consolider ses perspectives d’alliances. « Le Parti populaire a engagé un jeu politique et discursif à l’égard du Maroc pour satisfaire l’extrême droite espagnole et rallier une partie de son électorat », analyse-t-il. Pour autant, il ne s’attend pas à une dégradation durable des relations entre les deux pays. Les compromis imposés par la formation d’une coalition gouvernementale pourraient, selon lui, contribuer à atténuer les positions exprimées pendant la campagne. « Une fois le gouvernement installé et après un ou deux mois d’exercice du pouvoir, les choses reviendront à la normale », pronostique-t-il, écartant ainsi le scénario d’une détérioration substantielle des relations maroco-espagnoles. Sánchez, un pari sur le charisme et les alliances indépendantistes Si le Parti populaire semble bénéficier d’une dynamique favorable dans les sondages, les perspectives du Parti socialiste ouvrier espagnol (PSOE) de Pedro Sánchez ne sont pas pour autant définitivement compromises. Malgré l’usure de son gouvernement, fragilisé par la succession de scandales, notamment liés à des affaires de corruption, le chef de l’exécutif conserve des ressources politiques susceptibles de rebattre les cartes électorales. Abdelhamid Benkhattab décrit Pedro Sánchez comme un responsable politique particulièrement résilient, capable de revenir sur le devant de la scène alors que son avenir politique paraît compromis. « C’est un phénix. À chaque fois qu’on dit qu’il est terminé, il est toujours là sur la scène politique espagnole », observe-t-il, saluant également son intelligence politique et son charisme. Pour l’universitaire, les chances du PSOE reposent essentiellement sur deux leviers. Le premier tient à la capacité de Pedro Sánchez à mobiliser autour de sa personnalité et à conduire une campagne suffisamment efficace pour modifier les rapports de force. Le second concerne les alliances avec les formations indépendantistes, notamment basques et catalanes, dont le soutien pourrait s’avérer décisif dans la configuration parlementaire à venir. « Ce qui va déterminer les prochaines élections, ce sont les alliances avec les partis indépendantistes basques et catalans », estime-t-il. Ces formations ne disposeraient toutefois plus de la même force électorale que par le passé, ce qui pourrait compliquer la tâche du chef du gouvernement sortant. Selon Benkhattab, l’équation électorale du PSOE dépendra donc largement de sa capacité à préserver ou à reconstituer ces soutiens. Si les formations indépendantistes ne parviennent pas à obtenir une représentation parlementaire suffisante pour peser dans les négociations, les chances de Pedro Sánchez de conserver le pouvoir seraient considérablement réduites. Au-delà de l'affrontement entre la droite conservatrice et les socialistes, le scrutin espagnol se jouera ainsi autant sur les résultats électoraux que sur les tractations politiques qui suivront. Pour le Maroc, l’enjeu sera notamment de savoir dans quelle mesure les équilibres issus des urnes se traduiront dans la politique étrangère du prochain exécutif espagnol. items.title: Good night Olufemi Ajasa, you were more than a friend
items.description: By Taiwo George During the launch of the Converged Digital Newsroom of Media Trust Group, Alhaji Mohammed Idris, Minister of information and National Orientation, shared a personal story. While tracing the success story of the company, the Minister who was Special Guest at the occasion, narrated an encounter he had with Malam Kabir Yusuf, Chairman of the Board of Directors of the Media Trust Group. According to him, several decades ago, he and Media Trust Chairman had a sit-down session in Kaduna and Malam Yusuf told him about his dream of owning a successful media outfit, while he, the Minister, told Malam Kabiru of his own dream to be a Public Relations merchant. If there is anyone whom I shared my dream in this profession with, it was Olufemi. But because tomorrow is not promised to anyone, I unlike the Minister, would not have the opportunity to ever watch my late brother and colleague relieve a similar encounter in future. Kabi o osi! Femi and I shared many things in common. We attended same institution, though while he was at the Communication School of the Lagos State University (LASU) in Anthony, I was at the main campus in Ojo. We got admitted the same year and graduated same year. Our marital journey also has striking similarities. His wife and mine are both Mass Communicators. Our spouses were first colleagues before signing lifetime contract. While Femi met his wife at Uni, I met mine during the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) programme. At death, Femi was the Online Editor of Vanguard, I’m currently the Online Editor of Daily Trust. Both of us are not just proud sons of Lagos, but we share ancestral ties. This is why it’s still quite difficult to come to terms with his sudden demise. A man of few words. He moved on whenever he made his point. Femi was never the one who would bore you with a conversation. Each time we spoke on phone, he went straight to the point. The few times the conversation dragged I said let me quickly make this final point, he would respond, “Oya na!”, and follow up with, “Take care!” whenever I summarized my point. Something unusual happened on the eve of his death. We usually compared notes on so many issues, particularly work. I came across an information which had to do with his workplace and forwarded same message to him via WhatsApp but it didn’t deliver. An online Editor being offline during that period? I assumed he was in a place where network was bad, and would respond when he read the message until Monday morning when Victor Ogunyinka, our mutual friend, broke the news to me. I screamed and my wife who was coincidentally sleeping on the same couch Femi and his family sat when they attended the parlour party during my son’s third-year birthday, woke up. I told her what happened and she regained consciousness immediately. We went over a few memories with Femi and said prayers for the wife and kids he left behind. Where do I start sharing the memories from? I remember when I was to relocate from Lagos to Abuja, Femi heard the news before I shared with him. Having moved to the capital city years before I did, I sought his advice on a number of issues, especially accommodation. He didn’t like the choice I eventually made but I convinced him. Weeks later when he hosted a get together for me and a few colleagues, he joked that I got there far behind schedule because of the distance but I protested saying it was because of work and we all laughed it over. On a journalists’ WhatsApp Forum where a link on his obituary was dropped, a colleague wrote, “What a fine man! God rest his soul.” Talking about good looks, it’s common for people to command attraction in the early years of their youth but in the case of Femi, the charm improved as he aged. During the get together he organised for me upon relocation to Abuja, I almost didn’t recognize him. So cute and charming, I was like ’Abuja working well for you bro’, and he laughed asking which Ábuja? To prove that, he still didn’t lose his charm when Vanguard job took him back to Lagos. Femi touched so many lives. He was always on the lookout for opportunities to make life better for colleagues. When he clocked 40 four years ago, one of his mentees told me we needed to find a way to celebrate him. He came up with the idea of surprise package which clicked and quickly we got Funsho, his wife, into the picture. Because the mentee was in Lagos, I was the one who coordinated things after which he got in touch with Funsho who the package was delivered to and she kept it till he returned from work. The next morning, Femi called, “Taiwoooooo!! You ehn! Thanks man! Thanks man.” The conversation ended. Femi was a caring father who was involved in the lives of his children. As they made their way into the living room during the birthday, he watched them unlace their shoes and guided them to where they kept them. They also had chit chats that ended with smiles during the party. Not every father has such time in a busy era like this. Femi was a man who would praise you when the need arose and knock you if that’s what he felt you deserved. At a retreat organised three years ago, my boss asked me to get someone to review our brand, it was Femi who came through and he gave the team very practical and useful insights. After the 2023 election, Femi called me saying, “Taiwooooo, superb coverage! You guys really tried. I followed the fantastic job your team did. Daily Trust was number two in terms of coverage.” To him a brand whose name I won’t deliberately mention (not Vanguard) was number one and he gave his reasons. Other times, Femi would argue Vanguard’s dominance of the digital terrain and irrespective of my point, he would say emphatically, ‘Vanguard is number one!” When my platform was the talk of town over a controversial story, Femi called and asked, “Taiwo, what did you guys do there? You want to set this country on fire? Take time o!” The undeniable truth is that Femi loved his job and did it with passion. He gave his best to it and touched lives in the process. Every job has its challenges, but the aspect of the profession my late brother and I find ourselves in is no doubt demanding. It’s not a stroll in the park to manage the digital arm of a thriving newspaper. A decision taken within split seconds could ruin the brand’s hard-earned trust and you would be worse for it. The job is so jealous that at times, we cast headlines in the dream. I’ve lost the number of times an unexpected, unplanned activity disrupted a schedule planned for weeks or months. As Online Editor, you have to stay alert to guide your team and ensure things go smoothly. A colleague shared a video of Femi with his laptop beside him on the hospital bed and I connected with that immediately. I’ve travelled that route before. I remember when I was trapped in the hospital for days but still couldn’t let go of my laptop. My older son fell ill so the mother rushed him to hospital and I joined them after work. As of the time I got there, my younger son had also started showing symptoms. The matron advised that he should be taken away immediately to prevent the situation from getting worse. The responsibility of taking care of him fell on me but as my wife walked out with my younger son, I signalled her to wait outside. I needed something from the car, my laptop. Back to Femi, in that video, he said he was on drip and needed to rest before for a few hours before getting back to work. We’ve lost many colleagues recently. In August, it was Otunba Dotun Oladipo, who collapsed at work and gave up in the hospital. In September, it was Felix Onigbinde who also slipped into coma while on duty. Death is an inevitability for all mortals, that we know; but what about these untimely deaths? I think it’s high time we found a way to sort out work-life balance. Many questions racing through my mind over my friend’s demise. Was it substandard treatment? Did he ignore warning signs? Was he too busy to take care of his health? Does this have spiritual undertone? What happened to Femi? We can’t question God. I never imagined not having Femi around in the next 30 years but such is life: here today, gone tomorrow. I’ve been following the drama trailing the death of gospel singer Olayemi Bayonle, better known as Toluwanisings, not knowing that death was lurking around the corner. Sleep well, my friend and brother. Ki Oluwa te e si afefe rere. Ishe owo re oni baje o. Your son will tell your story someday, good night. The post Good night Olufemi Ajasa, you were more than a friend appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Snub against England at 2026 World Cup hurt me – Thomas-Asante
items.description: Ghana international Brandon Thomas-Asante said he was left disappointed in Carlos Queiroz’s decision to not use him in the Black Stars’ 2026 World Cup game against England. Having played a key role in Ghana’s win over Panama, Thomas-Asante was hoping to star for the Black Stars against the Three Lions. However, the Portuguese coach had other ideas, opting to leave the Coventry City man on the bench for the entirety of the game, a decision the forward admits was difficult to live with. “I was thinking this is the game I’m targeting. Like, everything I’m doing is in alignment with performing and showing that I’m one of the best players in the world; that’s what I want to do and what I want to be showing. “And it didn’t, of course; it didn’t come to pass in that time. I’m sure it hurts. And, you know, it did hurt. It was a hard one to take,” he told Joy Sports. Thomas-Asante also revealed he had approached the former Ghana boss to share his displeasure while urging the coach to trust him more. “I just had to keep my head down and keep working. As a player, sometimes I feel like I’m coming into my senior years now, so there are conversations that can be had. And I politely said to the manager as well after that game, I think you can trust me more to be a difference-maker on this team. “And sometimes when you say these things, maybe it’s taken well, maybe it’s not. But I think, the way I was raised, you go about things as a man, you communicate well, and you’re respectful. But you let your opinion; you talk when you need to talk. It was through my desire for wanting to serve the nation and to perform at the World Cup. So, yeah, it was tough,” he added. The Coventry City man featured in the Black Stars’ games against Somalia in the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) qualifiers, where the team picked up six points from both games.

items.title: GPNet celebrates member Nii Adjei Mensahfio on winning the GJA Best Online Documentary Award
items.description: The Ghana Photojournalist Network (GPNet) has congratulated its member, Nii Adjei Mensahfio, on winning the Best in Online Documentary award at the recently held Ghana Journalists Association (GJA) Media Awards, describing his achievement as a source of pride for the network. Mr Mensahfio, a freelance journalist, received the recognition for his documentary, “Poaching, Bush Burning: Mole National Park’s Conservation Scars”, which exposes the threats facing wildlife and the natural environment at the Mole National Park. President of the network, David Andoh, commended the award-winning journalist for his achievement and encouraged him to continue producing impactful work. “He has done well; he has made us proud, and he should continue to work to achieve more for himself and also for the network,” he said. Mr Andoh expressed confidence that the award would be the beginning of more achievements for Mr Mensahfio and urged other members to work hard towards winning recognition at both local and international levels. For Mr Mensahfio, the award was a mixture of surprise, uncertainty and fulfilment, particularly as he had set himself the goal of winning a GJA award. Recounting how he received the news, he said a colleague, Ridwan Karim Dini- Osman of EIB Network, first congratulated him through a WhatsApp message. “I was a bit shocked. I said, ‘wow, okay., Then in a moment I was like, ‘okay, so I won the award’,” he recalled. He said the moment became even more special because his mother was present at the ceremony to witness his achievement. “After the day, it was all pride and achievement. When I say pride, I don’t mean ‘arrogant’. I mean pride in the sense that I was happy and fulfilled with my work and the results it came with,” he said. Mr Mensahfio said his interest in documentary photography and commitment to climate journalism inspired him to investigate the conservation challenges at Mole National Park. The story emerged during a training programme with the Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development (CJID), where participants were required to pitch story ideas for a grant. Concerned about poaching, hunting and the burning of vegetation within the park, he decided to use his camera and writing skills to draw attention to the threats facing Ghana’s wildlife. “I find myself enjoying photographic living. I’m mostly interested in documentary photography. I enjoy being around new people, new environments, new worlds,” he said. One of the most disturbing experiences during the project was seeing an elephant that had lost its tusk, an encounter that reinforced his determination to tell the story. Although he initially hoped the documentary would attract widespread attention, it did not; however, the GJA recognition shed more light on the story, sparking renewed public interest, with more people requesting links to the work. He particularly commended MyJoyOnline and Daily Gist for publishing the documentary and helping give it visibility. “I want to give a big shout-out and a big thank you to MyJoyOnline and Daily Gist for giving the story life without subjecting me to any rigorous interrogation,” he said. He praised MyJoyOnline for publishing the story with its photographs and captions arranged as he had submitted them. He expressed hope that the award would draw further attention to the conservation challenges at Mole National Park and encourage meaningful interventions. Beyond the recognition, Mr Mensahfio called on corporate organisations, development partners and individuals to support photojournalists, particularly those documenting environmental and social issues. He said the high cost of cameras, lenses and other equipment, coupled with limited funding, continued to make field assignments difficult. He cited the support of an experienced colleague, photojournalist Gershon Gbeve, who lent him an expensive lens for the Mole National Park assignment as he did not own one and could not afford one. “We really need agencies and corporate Ghana to come on board and support people like me in the photojournalistic sector,” he appealed. Mr Mensahfio also disclosed that his agency, ClimeScape Africa, a nonprofit providing free photography and videography training for young Africans interested in climate reporting at a global standard, is rolling out an initiative aimed at equipping young people with the requisite skills to document environmental challenges and the natural world through accurate and impactful visual storytelling. The initiative, he intimated, is being carried out in partnership with Italian-based nonprofit – Associazione Culturale Vurria, and expressed openness to sponsorship and every other form of support for the project. Encouraging emerging photojournalists to remain committed to their passion, he said: “Let your passion lead you, but let wisdom guide you.” The Ghana Photojournalist Network says his achievement should inspire other members to pursue excellence and use photography to tell stories that contribute to public awareness and national development. The Mole National Park is home to a vast number of wildlife species, including the Kob, also known as the African Antelope. Some elephants in the Mole National Park were found with at least one tusk out of place, raising suspicions of poaching attempts

items.description: The Board Chairman of MTN Group, Mcebisi Jonas, has reaffirmed the telecommunications and fintech giant’s commitment to continued investment in Ghana, describing the country as a key market within the Group’s operations. He gave the assurance during a meeting with Ghana’s Finance Minister, Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, in Accra on Wednesday, November 18, as part of activities marking MTN Ghana’s 30th anniversary. Mr Jonas, who was accompanied by MTN Ghana Chief Executive Officer, Stephen Blewett, highlighted the company’s contribution to economic growth and employment creation, adding that MTN remains committed to creating long-term value for Ghanaians. He also stressed the importance of collaboration between government and the private sector in advancing Ghana’s digital transformation. “Ghana has been an important part of MTN’s story for three decades, and our commitment to its future remains as strong as ever,” he said. He added that the company intends to translate its partnership with government into investments that improve connectivity, expand opportunities and support the country’s digital agenda. Dr Ato Forson welcomed the delegation and commended MTN for its sustained investment in Ghana’s telecommunications and digital financial services sectors. He noted that partnerships between government and the private sector are essential to driving sustainable economic growth and creating jobs. MTN’s Role in Ghana’s Development MTN Ghana began commercial operations in 1996, becoming a pioneer in the introduction of GSM mobile telephony in the country. Over the past three decades, the company has expanded beyond telecommunications into digital financial services and other areas of the digital economy. Its contributions include capital investment, tax payments, local shareholding through its listing on the Ghana Stock Exchange, and social interventions through the MTN Ghana Foundation. The latest engagement with the Finance Ministry forms part of a series of stakeholder meetings marking the company’s 30 years of operations. items.title: Revue de presse de ce vendredi 20 novembre 2026
items.description: Voici les principaux titres développés par la presse nationale de ce vendredi 20 novembre 2026 L'Opinion • Le ministère du Transport et de la Logistique et la GIZ ont récemment rendu publique une étude qui envisage un bonus-malus et des normes CO2 pour les voitures neuves au Maroc. Ces mesures pourraient modifier les prix et placer les automobilistes devant des choix difficiles. Selon les seuils retenus, certains modèles abordables pourraient devenir plus chers, incitant des ménages à conserver leur ancien véhicule plus longtemps. Les expériences française et suédoise montrent que ces dispositifs peuvent modifier la dynamique des ventes, mais aussi produire des effets inattendus sur les émissions et les finances publiques. • Une résolution internationale sur les technologies renforçant la protection de la vie privée (Privacy-Enhancing Technologies, PETs), portée par la Commission nationale de contrôle de la protection des données à caractère personnel (CNDP), a été adoptée lors de la 48e conférence annuelle de l'Assemblée mondiale pour la protection de la vie privée « Global Privacy Assembly »(GPA), tenue du 16 au 19 novembre à Bruxelles. La résolution, adoptée mardi, braque les projecteurs sur le rôle des PETs dans l'intégration de la protection des données, de la conception des développements technologiques à la promotion de la coopération internationale en passant par le renforcement de la responsabilité des acteurs. Son adoption consacre l'engagement de la CNDP et ses efforts au sein de la communauté internationale de la protection des données. Le Matin • Le Roi Mohammed VI, accompagné du Prince Héritier Moulay El Hassan, a présidé, mercredi au Palais Royal de Rabat, une séance de travail consacrée à la présentation de l' »Offre Maroc » et de la feuille de route pour le développement de l'industrie nationale de défense et de sécurité. Cette séance s'inscrit dans le prolongement des hautes orientations royales visant à doter le Royaume d'une base industrielle et technologique de défense, à même de consolider sa souveraineté défensive et de générer des opportunités de développement technologique, économique et social. • Le Roi Mohammed VI a adressé un message de félicitations au Président de la République de Lettonie, Edgars Rinkēvičs, à l'occasion de la fête nationale de son pays. Dans ce message, le Souverain a également salué la volonté des deux pays d'aller de l'avant dans le développement des relations bilatérales pour les hisser davantage afin de couvrir différents domaines, de manière à répondre aux aspirations des deux peuples et à servir leurs intérêts communs. L'Economiste • Après le succès de la retenue à la source sur l'IR et l'IS, le principe a été élargi à la taxe sur la valeur ajoutée via la loi de finances 2024. Le dispositif a connu de nouveaux réaménagements via le projet de loi de finances 2027. La mesure est destinée à lutter contre la fraude en matière de TVA, en particulier par le biais des factures fictives qui avaient coûté plusieurs milliards de dirhams au Trésor. Le principe, qui a permis de lutter contre la fraude à la TVA et d'améliorer les recettes fiscales, consiste à procéder à une retenue à la source par les clients. Al Bayane • L’ambassadeur, Représentant Permanent des Etats-Unis d’Amérique auprès des Nations Unis, Mike Waltz, a réaffirmé l’engagement du Président Donald Trump envers Sa Majesté le Roi Mohammed VI, que Dieu L’assiste, à savoir la reconnaissance par les États-Unis de la souveraineté du Maroc sur le Sahara. Intervenant lors d’une conférence de presse tenue à l’issue de sa rencontre, mardi à Rabat, avec Nasser Bourita, ministre des Affaires étrangères, de la Coopération africaine et des Marocains résidant à l’étranger, le haut responsable américain a souligné que « la résolution historique 2797 du Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies, adoptée l’année dernière, a établi le cadre permettant de faire avancer les négociations et de résoudre ce différend de longue date ». Bayane Al Yaoum • Le nombre de bénéficiaires du programme d'aide direct au logement a atteint près de 131.000 depuis son lancement en janvier 2024, sur un total de 237.000 demandes remplissant les conditions d'éligibilité, a indiqué le ministre de l'Aménagement du territoire national, de l'Urbanisme, de l'Habitat et de la Politique de la ville, Porte-Parole du gouvernement, Samir Belfkih. En réponse à une question orale sur ce programme à la Chambre des conseillers, le ministre a précisé que le gouvernement a pris une mesure d'urgence pour accompagner la hausse des demandes, en injectant 600 millions de dirhams (MDH) en deux tranches de 300 MDH chacune, ce qui a permis de traiter environ 3.700 dossiers en attente de bénéficier dudit programme. Al Ittihad Al Ichtiraki • L’Agence du bassin hydraulique du Sebou prévoit de lancer une étude approfondie visant à diagnostiquer les dysfonctionnements affectant 11 petits barrages relevant de son ressort territorial. Cette expertise aura pour objectif d’évaluer leur état, d’identifier les risques potentiels et de proposer les interventions nécessaires à leur entretien, leur valorisation et leur réhabilitation. Elle permettra également de déterminer les causes des éventuelles défaillances, qu’elles soient liées au vieillissement des matériaux de construction, à l’insuffisance de la maintenance, aux conditions d’exploitation, à des lacunes dans la conception ou la réalisation des ouvrages, ou encore à des phénomènes hydrauliques, géologiques et géotechniques. Al Ahdat Al Maghribia • Le Directeur général de la Sûreté nationale et de la Surveillance du territoire (DGSN-DGST), Abdellatif Hammouchi, et le lieutenant-général Abdullah Khalifa Al-Murri, commandant en chef de la police de Dubaï aux Emirats Arabes Unis, ont signé un mémorandum d’entente visant à promouvoir la coopération bilatérale dans le domaine sécuritaire pour l’ériger en partenariat durable au rang des relations stratégiques distinguées entre les deux pays frères. Selon un communiqué du Pôle DGSN-DGST, ce mémorandum trouve ses fondements et ses finalités dans l’accord de coopération signé entre le Royaume du Maroc et l’Etat des Emirats Arabes Unis le 17 mars 2015 dans le domaine de sécurité et la lutte anti-terroriste. Assahra almaghribia • Le Roi Mohammed VI a adressé un message de félicitations à José Maria Pereira Neves suite à sa réélection à la présidence de la République de Cabo Verde. Dans ce message, le Roi adresse ses chaleureuses félicitations au Président Pereira Neves « pour la confiance que le peuple caboverdien vous a témoignée, en vous réélisant à la Présidence de la République ». • Le ministère de l’Éducation nationale, du Préscolaire, de la formation professionnelle et de la qualification a publié une nouvelle circulaire ministérielle encadrant l’établissement des listes définitives des bénéficiaires de la prime accordée aux « établissements pionniers », dans les cycles de l’enseignement primaire et secondaire collégial, ainsi que le lancement du versement des montants qui leur sont dus. Cette mesure s’inscrit dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre de la feuille de route 2022/26 et vise à valoriser l’engagement des personnels impliqués dans ce modèle éducatif. items.title: Ghanaian passport services disrupted in the UK as Ghana High Commission battles server challenges
items.description: Ghanaians seeking to obtain their passports through the Ghana High Commission in London may have to wait longer than expected, following a technical problem affecting the Commission’s systems. The Commission says the disruption has affected its ability to process and issue passports within the usual timeframe, with applicants who completed their biometric registration before November 2, 2026, likely to be particularly affected. The current disruption comes after a similar occurrence in August 2026. In a public notice released on Thursday, November 19, 2026, the Commission disclosed that its technical team was working to fix the problem to enable it to resume normal passport operations. It has urged applicants awaiting their passports to bear with the Commission while the necessary technical interventions are undertaken. The High Commission has also apologised for the delays and inconvenience caused by the disruption.

items.title: Mondial U17 : les Lionceaux lancent leur campagne face aux Fidji
items.description: Les Lionceaux de l’Atlas font, ce vendredi 20 novembre, leur entrée en Coupe du monde U17 (Qatar-2026) lors d’un premier acte décisif qui les opposera aux Îles Fidji, sur la pelouse du terrain N°7 de l’Aspire Zone à Doha à 16h00 ( GMT). Dans un groupe H particulièrement disputé, la sélection marocaine fera son entrée en lice lors de cette rencontre fondatrice pour les protégés d’Ahmed Kantari, qui visent une entame parfaite dans cette compétition mondiale. Forte d'une qualification acquise de haute lutte lors de la Coupe d'Afrique des Nations U17 organisée à domicile, où elle a atteint les quarts de finale, l'équipe nationale U17 se présente avec un groupe solide et très prometteur. L'effectif, récemment officialisé par la FIFA, révèle une forte dimension internationale. Le Maroc s'appuiera sur de jeunes pépites évoluant dans de prestigieux centres de formation européens, à l'image d'Ibrahim Rabbaj (Chelsea), Ziyad Baha (Olympique de Marseille) et Adam Mouak (Paris Saint-Germain), ainsi que sur des solides talents formés par l’Académie Mohammed VI de football et la Renaissance Berkane. Face à eux se dressent les Îles Fidji. Qualifiés en tant que brillants représentants de l'Océanie, les Fidjiens feront figure de Petit Poucet de la poule, mais représenteront un adversaire à prendre avec le plus grand sérieux. Dans un tournoi où l'intensité physique et la fraîcheur mentale jouent un rôle crucial dès la phase de groupes, les insulaires chercheront à bousculer la hiérarchie en misant sur leur combativité et leur discipline tactique. Pour les Lionceaux de l’Atlas, l'enjeu de ce premier acte dépasse largement les trois points. Placé dans un groupe relevé qui compte également la redoutable équipe d'Espagne et la Chine, le Onze national n'a pas droit à l'erreur, car une victoire d'entrée permettrait non seulement d'engranger un capital confiance indispensable, mais surtout de se positionner idéalement pour la course à la qualification. L'objectif est donc clair pour cette génération talentueuse, faire aussi bien que le quart de finale de l'édition précédente et confirmer l'excellente dynamique globale du football marocain sur la scène internationale. items.title: Betway launches GHS1m Level Up promotion with 2026 Jetour Dashing as grand prize
items.description: Betway Ghana has launched a six-week promotion, Level Up, offering players a prize pool worth more than GHS1 million, including a brand-new 2026 Jetour Dashing as the grand prize. Running from November 17 to December 27, 2026, the campaign covers sports betting, slots and crash games, with players competing for weekly rewards and places in the final prize draws. Weekly prizes include cash rewards, free bets, free spins and free flights. The top 10 performers on each weekly leaderboard will also qualify for the final draws, where major prizes, including iPhone 18s and the 2026 Jetour Dashing, will be awarded. Speaking at the launch, Betway Ghana Country Manager Jolade Adeoye said the promotion reflects the company’s commitment to rewarding players and improving their gaming experience. “Level Up is all about rewarding our players with one of our biggest year-end promotions,” said Jolade. “From weekly cash prizes and free bets to the chance to drive away in a brand-new 2026 Jetour Dashing, we’re giving players more ways to win while enjoying the games they love. We’ve also designed the promotion to be simple and accessible, making it easy for players to participate and track their progress throughout the campaign.” Adeoye also emphasised the importance of responsible gambling as Betway marks Responsible Gambling Month in November. “We encourage all players to stay in control of their spending and use the responsible gambling tools available on our platform. Responsible gambling remains a key part of our commitment to providing a safe and enjoyable betting experience for all our players,” she added. The promotion ends on December 27, with the final prize draw and grand prize handover scheduled for December 31, 2026. With more than GHS1 million in prizes at stake, Betway’s Level Up campaign is set to offer players across Ghana several opportunities to win as the year draws to a close.

items.title: Xi, Trump et Poutine : qui gagne quoi du sommet à trois ?
items.description: Arrivés à leur sommet inédit avec des objectifs différents, les présidents américain, chinois et russe en ressortent chacun avec des motifs de satisfaction. Xi Jinping a projeté une image de sérénité, Vladimir Poutine peut se sentir renforcé, tandis que Donald Trump occupe la scène malgré sa débâcle électorale. Alors qui a gagné quoi du sommet de jeudi à Shenzhen, dans le sud de la Chine. Xi, au centre du jeu Le président chinois disposait d'une occasion de placer son pays sur un pied d'égalité avec les États-Unis au cœur de la diplomatie mondiale, tout en projetant une image d'arbitre des débats. L'exercice n'était pas sans risque, notamment concernant la position de Pékin concernant la guerre entre la Russie et l'Ukraine. Pékin a en effet refusé de condamner ce conflit, s'attirant les critiques des pays occidentaux qui l'accusent de soutenir tacitement Moscou. « Xi s'est positionné au centre de l'événement, en tant qu'acteur central et initiateur de rencontres entre grandes puissances. Cette mise en scène renforcera sa stature politique » , souligne Ryan Haas, chercheur au sein de la Brookings Institution. Une « déclaration en faveur de la paix » , publiée par les trois pays à l'issue de la rencontre, reflète plusieurs positions défendues de longue date par la Chine, notamment sa volonté de réformer les institutions internationales, telles que l'ONU. « En parvenant à un consensus stratégique, (ces pays) peuvent stimuler une coopération multilatérale plus large et orienter la fonte de l'ordre mondial et des valeurs internationales », commente Wang Yiwei, directeur de l'Institut des affaires internationales à l'Université Renmin de Chine, à Pékin. Trump : de l'éclat, peu de résultats Le président américain espérait marquer des points sur le plan diplomatique après la débâcle de son camp aux élections de mi-mandat, qui a réduit sa marge de manœuvre pour ses deux dernières années à la Maison Blanche. Son déplacement a bien commencé : rompant avec des décennies de protocole pour les dirigeants chinois, Xi Jinping l'a accueilli personnellement à l'aéroport de Shenzhen lors d'une cérémonie en grande pompe. Mais au-delà d'une photo historique aux côtés de deux dirigeants qu'il couvre depuis longtemps d'éloges, il est difficile de savoir si Donald Trump a remporté la moindre victoire politique significative. © AFP Il est frappant de constater qu' « aucun nouvel accord » n'a été conclu entre les trois puissances, relève Chong Ja Ian, professeur à l'Université nationale de Singapour. Le format de la rencontre « laisse entrevoir la mise en place d'un système dans lequel Pékin, Moscou et Washington dicteraient leur conduite au reste du monde (…). Et compte tenu des liens étroits entre Pékin et Moscou, Washington pourrait se retrouver en position de faiblesse » , ajoute-t-il. Alors que la Maison Blanche avait dit espérer des discussions de fond sur le contrôle des armes nucléaires, la déclaration commune se contente d'annoncer un « dialogue » sur les « risques nucléaires » , une formulation vague qui n'engage pas préciser les trois pays à des réductions de leurs arsenaux. « Le président Trump revendiquera une victoire politique quel que soit le résultat de la rencontre » , relativise auprès de l'AFP Peter Loge, directeur de l'Ecole des médias et des affaires publiques de l'Université George Washington. « Reste à savoir si quelqu'un d'autre partagera cet avis », dit-il. Poutine : une place à la table des puissantes Au vu de la population et du poids économique de la Russie par rapport à la Chine et aux Etats-Unis, Vladimir Poutine aurait pu venir à Shenzhen avec un statut de second rang. Mais la bonne entente constatée avec Xi et Trump lui a donné, en dépit des tentatives des Occidentaux de l'isoler depuis qu'il est entré en guerre contre l'Ukraine en février 2022, un rôle plus conséquent, encore renforcé par la tenue de ce sommet sans précédent. « Les États-Unis et la Russie ont tous deux manifesté leur intérêt pour cette réunion trilatérale, tandis que la partie chinoise s'est apparemment montrée relativement réticente », explique à l'AFP Chim Lee, analyste de l'Economiste Intelligence Unit. « Le fait que la Chine en confirme la valeur signifie que ce dispositif a de très fortes chances de se poursuivre », atténuant toute incitation pour Trump à prendre ses distances avec la Chine et la Russie, ajoute-t-il. Pour Wu Xinbo, doyen de l'Institut d'études internationales de l'université Fudan de Shanghai, ce format montre que les États-Unis « ne peuvent plus dicter les affaires internationales » et doivent traiter la Russie et la Chine « sur un pied d'égalité ». The post Xi, Trump et Poutine : qui gagne quoi du sommet à trois ? appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .
