items.title: Ghanaians share simple acts of kindness they plan to spread this Christmas
items.description: As the Christmas season approaches, some Ghanaians are looking beyond the usual festivities, identifying simple ways to make the season more meaningful for others. In a Joy FM vox pop, respondents shared plans to show kindness through gifts, food and other gestures aimed at making someone happy during the festive period. Raymond Asante said he intends to buy a live chicken for a friend as his way of spreading kindness. “One act of kindness that I want to do this Christmas is to buy a live chicken for my friend,” he said. Princess Appong also plans to brighten someone’s Christmas by buying them a T-shirt. “One act of kindness I plan to do this Christmas is to buy someone a T-shirt,” she said. For Edwina Cobbinah, the season presents an opportunity to support someone with clothing, gifts or food. “I plan on giving out clothes and gifts to people. Either I do that or I give out foodstuff to a particular person I have in mind,” she said. Their plans reflect different ways people can express generosity during the festive season, from giving practical items to sharing food with someone in need. While Christmas is often associated with food, new clothes, gifts and celebrations, the responses suggest that small gestures can also make the season memorable. Joy FM is inviting listeners to share their own thoughts on the question through its social media platforms. Joy FM lines up festive programmes Beyond the conversations around kindness, Joy FM has announced a lineup of programmes and activities for the Christmas season. They include the Festival of Nine Lessons and Carols, Colours of Christmas, Family Party in the Park and the 90s Jam. The activities form part of the station’s festive-season offerings for its listeners.

items.title: One in three countries does not measure its air pollution, global report finds
items.description: One in every three countries in the world has no government system for measuring air pollution, leaving nearly one billion people without official information about the air they breathe, a new global report has found. The report, 2026 Open Air Quality Data: The Global Landscape, was released on 16 November by OpenAQ, a non-profit that runs the world’s largest open-source, open-access database of outdoor air quality measurements. It examined 198 countries, including the 193 UN member states. It found that 67 per cent of countries (two in every three) conduct or sponsor continuous air quality monitoring, up from 64 per cent in 2024. That leaves 65 countries with no evidence of government monitoring. Nearly one billion people live in them (roughly one in every eight people on Earth), and seven in 10 of those people live in low-income or lower-middle-income countries. “You can’t fix what you don’t measure, and right now a third of the world’s governments are flying blind on one of the biggest threats to public health,” said Jane Burston OBE, Founder and CEO of the Clean Air Fund. The threat is large. The State of Global Air 2025 report by the Health Effects Institute found that air pollution caused 7.9 million deaths in 2023, about one in every eight deaths worldwide. The Air Quality Life Index (AQLI), produced by the Energy Policy Institute at the University of Chicago (EPIC), estimates that air pollution cuts the average person’s life short by 1.9 years. Many of the countries without monitoring are places where air pollution takes a heavy toll. The report lists the 18 most populous of them. In all of them, air pollution is among the top eight risk factors for death and disability, and in seven it ranks first or second. Across these 18 countries, outdoor particle pollution was linked to about 183,000 deaths in 2023 (about 500 a day), according to State of Global Air estimates cited in the report. Twelve of the 18 are African, and they account for about 82,000 of those deaths. Among the African countries, Algeria recorded the most deaths (19,800), followed by Sudan (18,600). In the Democratic Republic of the Congo, home to about 113 million people, the AQLI estimates that people lose 2.7 years of life to particle pollution, the highest among the 18. Many of the most harmful pollutants cannot be seen or smelled. PM2.5 particles are about 30 times smaller than the width of a human hair, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency, and carbon monoxide is a colourless, odourless gas, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). The only way to know if the air meets the WHO guideline of 5 micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic metre is to measure it. The report notes that when the United States published data from monitors at its embassies abroad, fine particle pollution fell substantially in those cities, and that after the monitoring was halted in 2025, local pollution levels rose. Sub-Saharan Africa has the biggest gap of any region, with 56 per cent of its countries (more than half) not monitoring air quality. Yet the region is also changing fastest. Eight of the 11 countries that started monitoring since 2024 are African: Benin, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, The Gambia, Libya, Sierra Leone, Eswatini and Togo. In Togo, authorities recently developed national standards, with consultations underway to bring air-quality considerations into development planning. The Project Coordinator Lantam Djeri-Wake says the country is working to monitor air quality in more than 10 cities using both reference-grade monitors and low-cost sensors. “In Togo, the government has demonstrated its commitment to improving air quality through the Togo Air Quality Project (PQAT), which aims to monitor air quality in 11 cities using a combination of reference-grade monitors and low-cost sensors.” – Lantam Djeri-Wake Ghana monitors its air and shares the data, but not in a fully open way. According to the report, Ghana’s data do not include station-specific locations and cannot be accessed programmatically, that is, downloaded automatically by computer software. The report found that 61 per cent of countries share air quality data with the public, but only 33 per cent (one in three) share it in a fully open way, meaning it is detailed, timely, tied to exact locations and easy for computers to download. “The fastest route to clean air is to ensure everyone has access to information about air quality and can apply their expertise to reducing air pollution, yet only a third of countries give the public full, easy access to the air quality data they collect, and a third aren’t collecting data at all,” said Chris Hagerbaumer, Executive Director of OpenAQ. The number is growing, though. Countries sharing data fully openly rose from 45 in 2022 to 54 in 2024 and 65 this year, an increase of 20 countries that the report describes as statistically significant. “We hope the slow, but steady, progress toward data transparency will accelerate in the coming years,” Hagerbaumer said. The report urges every government to measure air quality, even starting with a single PM2.5 monitor, and to share the data fully openly. It calls on funders to back less-resourced governments and require open data, citing the EPIC Air Quality Fund as an example. “A relatively small investment in less-resourced countries can close data gaps, and when we fund monitoring, we should make sure the data is shared openly,” Burston said. Acting on air pollution can also pay off. The Hidden Assets report by the UN Environment Programme and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition found that every US$1 invested in measures that tackle air pollution and climate change together brings back about US$15 in economic benefits. END.

items.title: More than half of African countries do not measure their air pollution, report shows
items.description: More than half of Africa’s 54 countries have no government system for measuring air pollution, according to an analysis of a new global report, even as the continent leads the world in setting up new monitoring. The report, 2026 Open Air Quality Data: The Global Landscape, was released on 16 November by OpenAQ, a non-profit that runs the world’s largest open-source, open-access database of outdoor air quality measurements. It assessed whether governments in 198 countries measure their air quality and share the data with the public. An analysis of the report’s country-by-country data shows that 29 African countries have no evidence of government air quality monitoring. Eight monitor but do not share their data publicly, 12 share it only partially, and just five share it in a fully open way: Cabo Verde, The Gambia and South Africa at national level, and Kenya and Nigeria through programmes in Nairobi City County and Lagos State. The report’s own regional figures put sub-Saharan Africa at the bottom globally, with 56 per cent of its countries (more than half) not monitoring air quality, compared with 4 per cent in Europe and Central Asia and none in South Asia or North America. Of the 13 countries worldwide that monitor but keep their data private or publish only summaries, eight are African. “Notably, seven in ten people living without government air quality monitoring are in low- or lower-middle-income countries. That means that the communities facing the worst pollution are the ones with the least information to act on it,” said Jane Burston OBE, Founder and CEO of the Clean Air Fund. Many of the African countries without monitoring carry a heavy pollution burden. Twelve of the 18 most populous high-risk countries without monitoring listed in the report are African. Together, outdoor particle pollution was linked to about 82,000 deaths in these 12 countries in 2023 (about 225 a day), according to State of Global Air estimates cited in the report. Algeria recorded the most deaths (19,800), followed by Sudan (18,600) and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (11,400). In the DR Congo, home to about 113 million people, the Air Quality Life Index (AQLI) estimates that people lose 2.7 years of life to particle pollution. In Zambia the figure is 2 years and in Angola 1.8 years. The AQLI’s 2025 update found that people in the most polluted parts of Central and West Africa lose up to five years of life. Even where African governments do monitor, coverage is often thin, the report says. Much of Kenya’s monitoring is concentrated in Nairobi County, Madagascar’s in Antananarivo, and Eswatini has one publicly identifiable sensor. Some networks have also collapsed. Algeria’s national network fell into disuse and was not revived when international support to restore it failed to materialise. Algeria and Mozambique were both monitoring in 2024, but the report found no evidence that they still were in 2026. Yet Africa is also changing faster than anywhere else. Eight of the 11 countries that started monitoring since 2024 are African: Benin, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, The Gambia, Libya, Sierra Leone, Eswatini and Togo. In Guinea, which does not yet have a government network, a research centre installed the country’s first air quality sensors in 2025 as a pilot. In Togo, authorities recently developed national standards, with consultations underway to bring air-quality considerations into development planning. The Project Coordinator Lantam Djeri-Wake says the country is working to monitor air quality in more than 10 cities using both reference-grade monitors and low-cost sensors. “In Togo, the government has demonstrated its commitment to improving air quality through the Togo Air Quality Project (PQAT), which aims to monitor air quality in 11 cities using a combination of reference-grade monitors and low-cost sensors,” Djeri-Wake said. Some of Africa’s poorest countries are leapfrogging. The report notes that low-income countries including The Gambia, Sierra Leone, Ethiopia, Somalia and Uganda are using modern data platforms and international partnerships. The Gambia and Nigeria’s Lagos State now meet all the criteria for fully open data, having fallen short in 2024. Kampala City in Uganda and Nairobi City County in Kenya both rely on AirQo, a monitoring network based at Makerere University, to make their data downloadable. Ghana monitors its air and shares the data, but not in a fully open way. According to the report, Ghana’s data do not include station-specific locations and cannot be accessed programmatically, that is, downloaded automatically by computer software. The report urges every government to measure air quality, even starting with a single PM2.5 monitor, and to share the data fully openly. It calls on funders to back less-resourced governments and require open data, citing the EPIC Air Quality Fund as an example. “A relatively small investment in less-resourced countries can close data gaps, and when we fund monitoring, we should make sure the data is shared openly,” Burston said. The returns could be high. The Hidden Assets report by the UN Environment Programme and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition found that every US$1 invested in measures that tackle air pollution and climate change together brings back about US$15 globally, and about US$26 in southern Africa, the highest return of any region.

items.title: Collision maritime au large de Boffa : deux pêcheurs disparus (BAM)
items.description: Un nouvel accident maritime impliquant une barge opérant pour le compte de Bel Air Mining SAS (BAM) s’est produit dans la nuit du jeudi 19 novembre 2026 au large de Boffa. Le bilan provisoire fait état de deux pêcheurs portés disparus après une collision avec une pirogue de pêche artisanale. Cet accident intervient après deux précédents épisodes impliquant les opérations maritimes de la compagnie minière, dont un naufrage ayant provoqué une importante pollution des eaux marines en 2023. Selon un communiqué officiel de Bel Air Mining SAS, une barge opérant pour le compte de la société dans le cadre de ses activités de transbordement est entrée en collision avec une pirogue de pêche artisanale au large du port du Cap Verga, dans la préfecture de Boffa. La compagnie indique qu’une équipe conjointe composée de personnel de BAM et de l’entreprise CRCC-17 s’est immédiatement déployée sur les lieux pour porter secours aux victimes. « Une personne a pu être repêchée et prise en charge par l’équipe médicale de la clinique de Bel Air Mining. En revanche, deux autres occupants de l’embarcation demeurent introuvables », précise le communiqué. Les recherches se poursuivent en collaboration avec les ports de pêche environnants, sous la coordination des autorités administratives et maritimes compétentes, alertées dès les premières heures suivant le drame. Parallèlement, une enquête administrative et technique a été ouverte afin de déterminer les circonstances exactes de l’accident, ajoute la compagnie. Un précédent accident meurtrier en février 2026 Ce nouvel accident rappelle une autre collision survenue le 13 février 2026, dans les mêmes eaux, entre une barge appartenant à Bel Air Mining et une pirogue de pêche artisanale. L’embarcation transportait neuf personnes. Huit pêcheurs avaient été secourus grâce notamment à la mobilisation des pêcheurs du port de Koukoudé. Le neuvième occupant, identifié dans les premières informations comme Ibrahima Sory Sylla, était porté disparu. L’incident avait suscité des réactions au sein des organisations professionnelles de pêche et de la Chambre des Mines de Guinée. Une enquête avait également été annoncée pour établir les circonstances de cette collision. Le naufrage d’une barge et une importante pollution en 2023 Mais les incidents impliquant les opérations maritimes de Bel Air Mining ne datent pas de cette année. Le 10 juin 2023, la barge Terrang 3002, affrétée par la compagnie minière, avait chaviré au large de Boffa alors qu’elle transportait environ 7 502 tonnes de bauxite. Le naufrage avait entraîné le déversement de cette cargaison dans les eaux marines, soulevant de sérieuses préoccupations environnementales. À la suite de cet accident, les autorités guinéennes avaient infligé à Bel Air Mining une pénalité de 60,215 milliards de francs guinéens, notamment pour pollution des eaux marines et défaut de déclaration de l’incident. Ce précédent avait mis en lumière les risques environnementaux associés aux opérations de transport et de transbordement de la bauxite sur le littoral guinéen. La sécurité maritime au cœur des interrogations Avec ce nouvel accident du 19 novembre 2026, Bel Air Mining se retrouve une nouvelle fois au centre d’interrogations concernant la sécurité de ses opérations maritimes au large de Boffa. En l’espace de trois ans, les activités maritimes liées à la compagnie ont ainsi été associées à trois épisodes préoccupants : un naufrage ayant provoqué une pollution maritime en juin 2023, une collision avec une pirogue de pêche artisanale en février 2026 et une nouvelle collision, neuf mois plus tard, ayant fait deux disparus. Ces événements, même s’ils sont de nature différente et que les responsabilités doivent être établies par les enquêtes compétentes, posent la question des dispositifs de prévention des accidents, de l’entretien des barges, de la signalisation des zones de navigation et de la sécurisation des couloirs empruntés simultanément par les navires miniers et les pêcheurs artisanaux. Les autorités maritimes et minières sont notamment attendues sur les conclusions des enquêtes et sur les éventuelles mesures correctives destinées à prévenir de nouveaux drames. Pour l’heure, les recherches se poursuivent pour retrouver les deux pêcheurs disparus dans la collision du 19 novembre. Leurs familles restent dans l’attente, tandis que les circonstances exactes de ce nouvel accident restent à élucider.

items.title: Pakistan cruise to eight-wicket win over Sri Lanka to seal Test series 1-0
items.description: Pakistan wrapped up an eight-wicket victory over Sri Lanka in the second and final Test, chasing down a target of 90 in just 13 overs to seal the two-match series 1-0 on Friday. The hosts needed only 90 minutes on the fourth morning to complete the job after Mohammad Abbas dismissed the last Sri Lankan batter to end the visitors’ second innings at 316. It was Pakistan’s first Test win since they beat the West Indies in the summer and their first series victory in the ongoing World Test Championship cycle. The result was also just their third win in 11 matches in the current cycle, following draws against South Africa and the West Indies and series defeats in Bangladesh and England. The first Test against Sri Lanka, also played in Rawalpindi, had ended in a draw. Sri Lanka, who had resumed at 309-9, added seven runs before Asitha Fernando was trapped lbw for two by Abbas. Fernando reviewed the decision, but ball-tracking showed the delivery clipping the top of middle stump. Abbas finished with three wickets for 55 runs from 34 overs, including 15 maidens. Aamer Jamal also claimed three wickets for 67, while Razaullah took two for 116 and Saqib Khan one before being sidelined by a hamstring injury. Sri Lanka’s total left Pakistan needing 90 for victory, with Milan Rathnayaka unbeaten on 66 from 88 balls, including 12 fours. His fighting innings had been central to a recovery after the visitors were dismissed for 98 in their first innings and conceded a 227-run lead when Pakistan replied with 325. Pakistan’s pace attack had made full use of a green-tinged pitch to bowl Sri Lanka out cheaply on the opening day and put the hosts firmly in control. The tourists began their second innings 153 runs behind and slipped to 10-2, but half-centuries from Kusal Mendis (53), Sonal Dinusha (54) and Rathnayaka helped them reach 316 and avoid an innings defeat. Their 235-run effort on the third day briefly revived the contest, although the eventual target remained modest. Pakistan began the chase positively, with Azan Awais and Tayyab Arif putting on 18 for the opening wicket. The stand ended when Lahiru Kumara bowled Tayyab for 13, with the batter beaten by movement off the pitch after striking three fours. Azan was joined by Mohammad Taha, but the latter’s stay was brief. Asitha Fernando trapped him lbw for four, and Taha’s review failed as the ball was shown to be clipping leg stump. Pakistan were 37-2, but Sri Lanka could not build on the breakthrough. Aamer was promoted up the order and turned the chase into a brisk finish. He struck 34 not out from 22 balls, hitting five fours and a six, and added an unbroken 53 with Azan for the third wicket. Aamer attacked from the outset, taking boundaries off Fernando and Kumara before finishing the match with a four off Prabath Jayasuriya. Azan remained unbeaten on 32 from 36 balls, with five fours, as Pakistan reached 90-2 in 13 overs.

items.title: Fawzia Zouari : «Je suis une femme, arabe, tunisienne, musulmane et laïque»
items.description: Nous reproduisons ci-dessous le discours prononcé par l’écrivaine et journaliste tunisienne Fawzia Zouari, le 16 novembre 2026 à l’Hôtel de Ville de Paris, en recevant le Prix Laïcité Culture 2026. Et, bien sûr, il n'y avait aucun officiel tunisien dans la salle. Comme quoi, nul n'est prophète dans son pays. Cette reconnaissance vient s’ajouter à un parcours marqué par le journalisme, la littérature et les débats sur l’identité et la place des femmes dans la société. Fawzia Zouari est, rappelons-le, présidente du Parlement des écrivaines francophones (PEF). Mesdames, Messieurs, Merci infiniment pour ce prix que j’aimerais dédier au premier président laïque du monde arabe, Feu Habib Bourguiba et à mon pays, la Tunisie. Je m’appelle Fawzia Zouari. Je suis une femme, arabe, tunisienne, musulmane et laïque. Non, ce n’est pas un paradoxe. Car s’il est vrai que la laïcité demeure un concept confus dans la pensée arabo-musulmane et que l’islam politique se refuse à être laïc, rien n’empêche les musulmans de l’être. D’où mon réflexe – et celui de bien d’autres musulmans par le monde – de sonner l’alerte au quotidien contre le retour du religieux ; d’où mon inquiétude devant la crispation des mentalités, la résurgence de pratiques anciennes et le spectacle d’une laïcité malmenée, enfreinte, contestée ; devant des institutions désarmées face à une demande religieuse puissante et vindicative ; devant un féminisme à l’épreuve de l’islamisme en particulier, du fait religieux en général. Je dois dire que mener le combat de la laïcité n’est pas facile pour les musulmans laïcs dont je suis. Nous sommes pris entre plusieurs feux : il y a ceux, parmi les nôtres, qui nous traitent de «vendus» , de «harkis» , d’informateurs indigènes passés dans le camp de l’impérialisme occidental, ou de «musulmans de service» . Il y a les tenants d’une idéologie d’extrême Droite, en France comme ailleurs en Europe, qui fabrique la haine de l’islam et ne cesse de diaboliser les musulmans et de faire croire qu’un mahométan ne peut être qu’un croyant forcené et un handicapé de la laïcité. Il y a une pensée insidieuse qui se drape derrière les oripeaux de la République, et parfois de la laïcité, pour cacher sa haine de l’islam et des musulmans. Et un étendard idéologique qui croit tenir le «bon arabe» pour camoufler et légitimer toutes les formes de mépris à l’arrière-fond colonial. Ces discours qui empêchent d’ouvrir le champ d’une pensée libre Il y a une élite française de gauche, auto-proclamée avocate d’office du Musulman quels que soient ses torts. Des universitaires qui s’indignent de toute critique que nous osons formuler sur nos sociétés d’origine. Des sociologues qui nous traitent d’essentialistes, voire d’islamophobes tout musulmans que nous sommes. Des ethnologues qui présentent le mariage précoce, l’inégalité dans l’héritage ou l’exigence de virginité, comme des spécificités culturelles à respecter. Il y a également un contexte international qui signe le retour de l’impérialisme à la Trump, comme il y a un traitement médiatique, notamment de la question palestinienne, marqué par les deux poids deux mesures, qui pousse parfois même les musulmans laïcs dans leurs appartenances, voire leurs retranchements. Il y a la fermeture des frontières du Nord qui ne fait qu’augmenter le sentiment au Sud, d’une Europe qui nous tourne le dos et ne mérite pas qu’on défende ses valeurs. Enfin, il a les discours officiels, les visions électoralistes, la défense d’intérêts financiers, et la réaction timorée de politiques obnubilés par la peur de l’islam ou fascinés par le communautarisme. Ces discours me font mal à moi et à tout laïc musulman, où qu’il soit dans le monde. Discours d’accusation, de compassion ou d’apitoiement sur nous-mêmes. Discours qui nous empêchent d’ouvrir le champ d’une pensée libre et rénovatrice, de réfléchir sur nos sociétés, de sortir du statut d’objet d’histoire pour devenir sujet de notre histoire, ici comme ailleurs. C’est pourquoi défendre la laïcité se doit de dénoncer ces discours. Rappeler l’erreur qu’il y a en France à mépriser les musulmans tout autant que celle à faire de l’islam la norme, laissant entendre que tous les musulmans se sentent agressés par la moindre critique concernant leur foi. Admettre qu’un musulman français n’est pas obligé de choisir entre ses origines et sa citoyenneté, ni de céder aux chantages de ses coreligionnaires ou faire allégeance aveugle à son pays d’adoption. Sortir de ces discours, c’est avancer ensemble et plus vite vers une laïcité claire, assumée et débarrassée d’arrière-pensée. C’est clamer que la laïcité n'est pas un désenchantement du monde mais son réenchantement, la tentative de le débarrasser des ferments de guerre et de conflits générés principalement par les religieux, leurs légendes d’âge d’or et leurs mythes de retour. Sortir de l’emprise du dogme vers la logique humaine C’est pourvoir défendre sans filtre ni crainte une exception française qu’on se doit de promouvoir au rang de valeur universelle. C’est refuser l’imposture qui consiste à vouloir reformuler le religieux sur des bases modernes. Et dire combien il est bon, nécessaire, de sortir de l’emprise du Dogme vers la logique humaine. Sortir du récit théologique pour l’Histoire, de la récitation pour la réflexion. De fonder ou refonder un État de citoyens et non un État de croyants. Et surtout, de faire entendre la voix des femmes. Pourquoi les femmes ? Parce qu’elles sont un baromètre fiable pour évaluer la mainmise du religieux sur les affaires de la cité, l’adhésion ou non à une société de progrès et de liberté. La légitimation de la loi religieuse entraine la mise sous tutelle des femmes, au mieux leur maintien dans une zone grise du monde. Et quel est donc le levier à opposer à cette logique religieuse, si ce n’est la laïcité. Dès lors, défendre la laïcité, c’est s’engager tout naturellement dans un combat féministe. C’est se battre contre ceux qui ont pour objectif politique et culturel d’évincer la gent féminine de l’espace public ; se battre contre tous les clergés qui font du corps féminin un champ de batailles au service de leurs instincts de pouvoir et de violence. C’est dire une fois pour toute que la laïcité est la principale alliée des femmes. Et que notre avenir se joue sur cette bataille importante, fondamentale, historique. Et pour paraphraser Lysistrata d’Aristophane, affirmer que lorsque la guerre contre l’intégrisme -d’où qu’il vienne-, sera faite par les femmes, elle s’appellera la laïcité. Voilà notre révolution en attente. Celle qui signera non seulement la naissance de l'individu féminin sous tous les cieux, mais la liberté de conscience et l’égalité pour tous les êtres humains. La révolution qui posera la première pierre d’une civilisation universelle basée sur le respect de l’Homme et le souci de colmater les blessures et les doléances de l’histoire issues principalement des conflits religieux, qu’ils soient anciens ou récents. Mesdames et Messieurs, Je ne vous cache pas que j’ai entendu aujourd’hui, dans cette salle, des discours qui m’ont choquée et peinée, à tel point que je me suis demandée : Mais qu’est-ce que je fais ici ? Car il m’a semblé que la laïcité servait de tribunal et de procès contre l’islam et les musulmans. Si j’accepte aujourd’hui ce prix, c’est au nom d’une laïcité dont je me réclame et qui, par sa définition première, n’exclut aucune communauté, aucune minorité et se refuse à se complaire dans le rejet de l’Autre : l’islam et les musulmans, en particulier. Paris, 16 novembre 2026. * Le titre et les intertitres sont de la rédaction. L’article Fawzia Zouari : «Je suis une femme, arabe, tunisienne, musulmane et laïque» est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Musadik Malik arrives in New Delhi to attend SCO dialogue forum
items.description: Federal Minister for Climate Change and Environmental Coordination Dr Musadik Malik arrived in New Delhi on Friday to attend the SCO Civilisational Dialogue Forum. His visit is a first by a Pakistani minister since former foreign minister Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari attended the SCO meeting in the Indian state of Goa in May 2023, and two years after India’s Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar attended the bloc’s meeting in Islamabad in 2024. Musadik was received at the airport by Pakistan’s Chargé d’Affaires Saad Waraich, according to the Pakistan High Commission in India. Dr Malik will lead the Pakistan delegation at the forum, being held from Nov 20 to Nov 22. The gathering will bring together representatives from Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) member states to discuss issues related to civilisational dialogue and cultural understanding, the Foreign Office said in an earlier statement. “The government of Pakistan remains committed to promoting dialogue among civilisations and fostering people-to-people contacts within the SCO framework in a spirit of mutual respect,” the statement said. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi is also scheduled to address the “Civilisational Dialogue Forum” of the 10-member regional bloc. The forum was proposed by Modi at the SCO Council of Heads of State summit in Tianjin, China, in September 2025. Recent high-level engagements between Pakistan and India have largely taken place under the SCO framework; for instance, Bilawal’s visit in 2023 and Jaishankar’s in 2024. But neither visit had featured formal bilateral talks. More recently, India’s SCO National Coordinator Alok Dimri visited Islamabad in late September for a preparatory meeting ahead of the next SCO Council of Heads of State summit. “This is my first time on Pakistani soil; these SCO-related programmes will continue throughout the year and culminate in the Islamabad summit,” the Indian official told PTV News at the time. Pakistan has assumed the rotating chairmanship of the SCO Council of Heads of State for the 2026-27 term and is scheduled to host the organisation’s summit in Islamabad in August 2027. Relations between India and Pakistan have remained strained, particularly since the four-day military conflict in May 2025, with official engagement largely confined to multilateral forums. Additional input from AFP

items.title: Eastern NDC youth organiser backs Opong-Fosu for National Chairmanship
items.description: The Eastern Regional Youth Organiser of the National Democratic Congress (NDC), Richard Etornam Nyarko, has declared his support for former Local Government Minister Dr Akwasi Opong-Fosu in the party’s National Chairmanship race. Mr Nyarko said the NDC, as a governing party, needed stable and experienced leadership to manage its national affairs and maintain cohesion. He made the remarks on Thursday, November 19, 2026, when Dr Opong-Fosu and his campaign team met regional executives in Koforidua to begin the Eastern Region leg of his campaign tour. Sharing his position on the contest, Mr Nyarko said: “A party in power doesn’t need a chaotic leader.” He described Dr Opong-Fosu as “the right man for the job at this point in time”, citing the need for steady leadership within the party. Dr Opong-Fosu’s campaign is centred on disciplined leadership, institutional strength and cohesion within the NDC. Drawing on his experience as a former Local Government Minister, he is presenting himself as a candidate who can provide what the campaign describes as calm and purposeful leadership at the national level. The campaign has been engaging regional executives, former government appointees, Metropolitan, Municipal and District Chief Executives (MMDCEs), and grassroots party structures as it seeks support across the party. The Eastern Regional tour is scheduled to run from Thursday, November 19, to Saturday, November 21, 2026. The campaign team is expected to engage party stakeholders in Koforidua, Somanya, Asamankese, Oda, Nkawkaw, Tease and Ekye-Amanfrom. The tour follows previous campaign engagements in the Volta, Oti, Greater Accra and Central Regions, as well as a meeting with the NDC’s Majority Caucus in Parliament.

items.title: The weekend reset that makes your new week easier
items.description: By Josephine Agbonkhese There is something about the weekend that makes us realise just how much we have been carrying throughout the week. After days of juggling work, family responsibilities and other commitments, the weekend offers an opportunity to slow down, catch our breath and put a few things in order. Beyond sleeping in, watching our favourite shows or catching up with friends, the weekend is also a good time to prepare for the days ahead. A few simple activities can make the transition into a new week less stressful and more manageable. Tidy up your space You do not need an elaborate cleaning exercise. Start with the areas you use most. Clear the kitchen counter, arrange the living room, put away scattered clothes and organise your workspace. A tidy environment can make it easier to concentrate and settle into your daily activities. It also feels good to start Monday without a pile of unfinished chores staring back at you. Plan your outfits ahead Save yourself the morning rush by deciding what to wear before the week begins. Check your calendar, consider your appointments and put together outfits that suit your activities. Iron your clothes, arrange your shoes and accessories, and ensure everything is ready. If you have children, preparing their school uniforms can also save valuable time. It is an opportunity to rediscover pieces in your wardrobe and experiment with new combinations. Prepare a few meals After a long day at work, deciding what to cook can become another chore. A little meal preparation over the weekend can help. Wash and portion vegetables, prepare a stew or soup, cook basic ingredients or simply plan your meals for the week. You do not have to prepare everything in advance. Knowing what you intend to eat can save time, reduce food waste and discourage expensive last-minute purchases. Take a break from your screen If your weekdays involve computers, messages and endless social media scrolling, use part of the weekend to disconnect. Put your phone aside for a few hours. Read a book, take a walk, spend time with family or enjoy a quiet moment without feeling the need to document it online. Constant notifications can make it difficult to switch off mentally. Spending some time away from screens allows you to be more present and enjoy other activities. Review your finances A weekend reset is a good opportunity to review your spending. Check your account balance, look through recent transactions and consider the expenses coming up during the week. Set aside money for transportation, groceries, school needs and other commitments. A simple spending plan can help prevent unnecessary financial pressure. It is not about denying yourself life’s pleasures but about knowing what you have and how best to manage it. Make time for yourself Between work, family and social obligations, personal time can easily become an afterthought. Dedicate part of your weekend to something you genuinely enjoy. Visit a favourite restaurant, get your hair or nails done, exercise, listen to music, watch a movie or catch up with a friend. You could also spend an afternoon doing absolutely nothing. Remember, rest is not a reward you must earn after completing every task. It is essential to maintaining your well-being. Write down your priorities for the week Before Monday arrives, take a few minutes to think about what you need to accomplish. Write down your important tasks, appointments and deadlines. Identify the three things that deserve your attention first. Having a written plan gives you a clearer sense of direction and makes it easier to approach your responsibilities one step at a time. It also helps you distinguish between what is urgent and what can wait. Get enough sleep Proper rest is perhaps the most underrated part of a weekend reset. Staying up late to squeeze in another movie or finish unfinished chores can leave you struggling on Monday morning. Maintain a regular bedtime, reduce late-night screen time and create a comfortable sleeping environment. items.title: My Day, My Rights, My Future
items.description: Have you ever woken up and wondered what a child’s day looks like? Have you paused to imagine what goes through their minds, the dreams they have, and the challenges they face? Perhaps we see children every day, but how often do we take time to understand the world through their eyes? For some children, a day is filled with laughter, learning, friendship, and love from parents and significant others. Yet for many more, it comes with hunger, fear, neglect, and uncertainty. Sometimes, we take these little things for granted, forgetting that a safe home, quality education, a listening ear, and the freedom to play can mean everything to a child. Today, as we mark World Children’s Day 2026, let us reflect on some important questions: are we doing enough to give every child the childhood they deserve? How is the day of a child? Are their rights being protected? Are their voices heard? and How secured is their future? In Ghana, the everyday life of a child is nothing ordinary; it is a roller-coaster of events — from performing academic duties such as studying, to activities such as performing chores, playing, or basically just having fun. These moments may seem small and mundane, but they are not. They reflect whether a child’s access to education, right to identity, protection, health, and participation in decisions that affect their lives are being fulfilled. One of the basic ways we can actualise these rights is by presenting children with the right to identity. Birth registration is the very first affirmation of the identity a child holds. A child born in Ghana to Ghanaian parents is considered Ghanaian and, therefore, should be recognised as such. Birth registration, in my opinion, gives the child a legal identity and citizenship. Yet, in many rural communities and busy towns across the country, countless children grow up without this vital document simply because their parents could not easily access a Births and Deaths Registry after delivery. Years later, when that same child is ready, for instance, to acquire a Ghana Card or secure a scholarship, the absence of a birth certificate becomes a hindrance to such opportunities. A child who is not given the opportunity to go through a birth registration process is being deprived of his or her right to identity as a citizen of Ghana. I, therefore, urge parents, guardians, and stakeholders to ensure that every child is registered, since it forms part of their fundamental human rights as children. Another crucial right of children that cannot be overlooked is the right to education. As the saying goes, “Education is the key to success”— will denying a child the right to education not be depriving him or her of being successful in the future? Article 25, Clause 1 of the 1992 Constitution of Ghana states that “All persons shall have the right to equal educational opportunities and facilities.” “All persons” means it includes children. However, as an avid reader of the Junior Graphic, I’ve read and seen photos of children in the bustling streets and the lorry stations in the country during school hours, hawking sachet water, plantain chips, and other wares to support their families, while others in remote communities study under trees due to a lack of classroom blocks, while those who are fortunate to study in classrooms also lack furniture, textbooks and qualified teachers. It is our collective responsibility to ensure that every child of school-going age is provided with facilities in order to build a solid foundation for their future. Decision-makers, politicians, parents, community leaders, and most importantly, the government must invest in the education sector to provide quality education for children. These sayings, “The success of a child is the success of the whole nation,” and “The efforts of a country contribute to the success of a child”, stipulate that children are the future of every country, and governments must ensure that policies are put in place to enable them to realise their full potential to achieve Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 4. Violence against children is another critical issue that affects children not only in Ghana, but around the globe. Article 28, Clause 3 of the 1992 Constitution of Ghana also states that “A child shall not be subjected to torture or other cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.” My understanding of this statement is that, under no circumstances should a child be exposed to torture, child labour, or sexual and physical abuse. Sadly, in our communities, we still witness young children being subjected to harsh corporal punishment, tedious tasks, domestic and sexual abuse. The Wednesday, November 4-10, 2026, edition of the Junior Graphic reported that over 53,000 teen girls got pregnant in just seven months, and violence against girls and lack of sex education were the major causes. Children are supposed to be nurtured with absolute care and love, not only by parents and guardians, but also by the people around them. The love and care shown to us children help in the development of our mental and psychological well-being. Moreover, children should be given the opportunity to share their opinions on matters that affect them. In many homes and schools, the adage that “children should be seen and not heard” still silences young people, even when decisions are being made about their schooling, welfare, and future. Yet, when we are given platforms such as the Junior Graphic, school clubs, community durbars, or children’s parliaments to express ourselves, we offer honest solutions to the everyday challenges we face. These opportunities are like voices given to children to speak up and talk about their problems. We are given the opportunity to own our future by making decisions and sharing opinions. Media platforms, community leaders, parents, and guardians can come together to turn children’s voices into public action. I, Princess Enam Avoxe, the Winner of the 2025 Junior Graphic National Essay Competition organised by the Graphic Communication Group Ltd, strongly urge the Government of Ghana, stakeholders, and the world at large to put in efforts to ensure the rights of children are protected and their voices are heard. For a child saved today is a future generation secured. Princess Enam, Avoxe 2025 Junior Graphic Essay Competition Winner, Sonrise Christian High School, Ho.

items.title: Lahore once again ranks as world's most polluted major city as AQI crosses 400
items.description: LAHORE: Heavy smog pushed air quality in several Punjab cities into the hazardous category on Friday, with Lahore recording an hourly AQI reading of 465 between 7am and 8am, while Gujranwala and Multan registered readings of 661 and 641, respectively, according to real-time air quality data. Lahore’s historical hourly air quality graph classified the reading of 465 as hazardous, indicating extremely polluted conditions and serious health risks for residents. A separate ranking of Pakistani cities placed Gujranwala at the top with an AQI of 661, followed by Multan at 641 and Lahore at 426. Other Punjab cities also reported elevated pollution levels, including Sargodha (289), Sialkot (232), Rahim Yar Khan (228) and Bahawalpur (198). The readings indicate a widespread deterioration in air quality across Punjab, with several cities experiencing hazardous pollution levels that pose serious health risks, particularly to children, elderly people and those suffering from respiratory and cardiovascular diseases. Residents have been advised to minimise outdoor activities, keep windows closed, wear protective masks when going outside and use air purifiers indoors. Prolonged exposure to high concentrations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) can aggravate respiratory and cardiovascular conditions. The deterioration in air quality comes despite intensified enforcement operations by the Punjab Environment Protection and Climate Change Department against sources of pollution, particularly non-compliant brick kilns. According to departmental figures, enforcement teams conducted 84,370 inspections of brick kilns across the province between Jan 1 and Nov 18, demolishing 1,429 units, sealing 968 and registering 1,248 FIRs against violators. Fines totalling Rs178 million were also imposed. During the critical smog period from Sept 1 to Nov 18, the department conducted 29,999 visits, demolished 519 kilns, sealed 494 and registered 408 FIRs, besides imposing fines totalling Rs101.45m. In the first 18 days of November, enforcement teams conducted 7,509 visits, demolished 101 kilns, sealed 161 and registered 96 FIRs, while imposing fines totalling Rs27.6m. On Nov 18 alone, 552 brick kilns were inspected, 22 demolished and 19 sealed. Fourteen FIRs were registered and fines totalling Rs3.5m were imposed. The department has also introduced repeated inspections to monitor previously inspected kilns and identify units that resume environmentally harmful practices after initial enforcement action. Environment Protection and Climate Change Department Secretary Silwat Saeed has directed sustained field enforcement and coordination to address pollution at its sources, while Director General EPA Punjab Abdullah Nayyar Sheikh has maintained a zero-tolerance approach towards environmental violations. Meanwhile, Pakistan’s average PM2.5 concentration stood at 67.3 micrograms per cubic metre in 2025, nearly 14 times the World Health Organisation’s annual guideline of 5 micrograms per cubic metre, according to the 2025 World Air Quality Report. This concentration corresponded to an average AQI of 156, placing Pakistan among the world’s most polluted countries. The latest readings underline the continuing challenge of controlling air pollution in Punjab despite enforcement measures against industrial and other sources of emissions.

items.title: Three children orphaned in acid horror
items.description: *Three Lives Left in the Shadows of Domestic Violence and Sickle Cell Struggles, after murder and suicide By Adeola Badru For three children in Akufo, Ido Local Government Area of Oyo State, life has become a painful journey into uncertainty. In one devastating episode, they lost both parents—the two people they should have been able to depend on for love, protection, education and survival. Their tragedy is particularly heartbreaking because two of the surviving children reportedly battle recurrent sickle cell crises, requiring regular medication and medical attention. At a time when they need parental care more than ever, they have, instead, been left to confront grief, illness, financial hardship and an uncertain future. Their story is not merely about the death of two parents. It is about a family reportedly torn apart by years of domestic violence, a marriage allegedly marked by repeated abuse and three innocent children left to bear the consequences of circumstances beyond their control. The incident reportedly followed years of domestic violence. The husband, identified as 49-year-old Mr Lekan Adedeji, allegedly poured acid on his wife, 44-year-old, before ingesting the same corrosive substance. Both subsequently died. The couple had been married for more than 25 years, but what should have been a lifetime of companionship was, according to the woman’s family, characterised by repeated physical abuse and disagreements over childbearing, even after the health implications of their genetic compatibility became known. Speaking with Vanguard, Morufat Ashake, the deceased woman’s younger sister, who has taken custody of the children, recounted the painful circumstances surrounding the marriage and the events preceding the fatal attack. She explained that the couple were unaware of their genotype status when they married. It was only after their first three children began experiencing recurrent illnesses that they discovered the medical implications of their genetic compatibility. According to Ashake, Zainab eventually gave birth to six children, three of whom died from complications associated with sickle cell disorder. The surviving children are Rashida Adedeji, 20, who is SS; Folawe Adedeji, 17, who is AS; and Folahanmi Adedeji, six, who is also AS. Rashida and the youngest child reportedly experience recurrent health crises and require consistent medical attention. But the family’s medical challenges were not the only difficulties Zainab allegedly endured. Ashake said her sister suffered years of physical abuse from her husband, who reportedly continued insisting on having more children despite knowing the potential health implications. Eventually, Zainab reportedly found the courage to leave the matrimonial home, hoping to escape the violence. She had been away for about three months before the incident. Although members of the family had previously intervened and persuaded her to return, Ashake said her sister had reached a point where she could no longer endure the situation. Sadly, the decision that should have marked the beginning of a safer chapter in Zainab’s life did not prevent the tragedy that followed. A school fees invitation that ended in horror Ashake traced the circumstances surrounding the fatal encounter to December last year, when Lekan allegedly contacted his estranged wife under the pretext of giving her money for their second daughter’s West African Senior School Certificate Examination (WASSCE) fees. Believing the invitation concerned their daughter’s education, Zainab reportedly visited the house with Folawe and her youngest son, Folahanmi. According to her account, Lekan instructed Folawe to take her younger brother outside. The teenager remained in the compound, sweeping, when she suddenly heard her mother’s screams coming from inside the house. Alarmed, she attempted to open the door but was allegedly prevented from entering by her father. She alleged that Lekan subsequently poured acid over Zainab’s body and attempted to force her to drink the corrosive substance. Ashake further disclosed that before ingesting the substance, Lekan allegedly handed his mobile phone and the money intended for the children’s school fees to another person. Both victims required urgent medical attention. Despite efforts to save Zainab’s life, she eventually succumbed to her injuries on January 23. The family reportedly spent more than N4 million attempting to secure treatment for her. For the children, the incident meant losing their mother in particularly traumatic circumstances and subsequently being left without their father. An ageing grandmother, three children and an uncertain future Their maternal grandmother, 62-year-old Titilayo Ayoola, corroborated Ashake’s account, describing her daughter’s marriage as one marked by years of suffering. Ayoola now faces the enormous responsibility of caring for three grandchildren who have lost both parents, including two who reportedly require regular medical attention. At an age when she should ordinarily be enjoying some rest, she must now worry about medication, hospital bills, school fees and the emotional wellbeing of children struggling to comprehend their loss. Her concern reflects the difficult reality confronting the family. Love and determination may provide emotional support, but the children also need sustained financial assistance, medical care, educational support and psychological counselling. For Rashida, the eldest, the pain is compounded by uncertainty about what lies ahead. Folawe, 17, who reportedly witnessed the events preceding her mother’s death, also described the family’s predicament. Her experience is particularly distressing. At an age when she should be concentrating on her education and dreams, she is having to process a traumatic experience involving the violent loss of her mother. Their youngest sibling, six-year-old Folahanmi, must also grow up without the daily presence of either parent. The family previously lived in a four-bedroom flat built by Lekan in Akufo. However, the house that once accommodated the family has become associated with the violent incident that brought their marriage to a tragic end. A tragedy that demands society’s attention Beyond the immediate grief of the Adedeji family, the incident raises troubling questions about domestic violence and the protection available to victims seeking to escape abusive relationships. Marriage should never become a prison in which one partner lives in perpetual fear of the other. Neither should leaving an abusive relationship expose a victim to further danger. The family’s account also underscores the importance of genotype awareness, responsible family planning and access to proper medical counselling. For the three surviving children, however, these lessons come amid a reality far more painful than any public discussion can capture. They need help to continue their education, manage their medical conditions and recover from the emotional trauma of losing both parents. Their grandmother and maternal aunt have assumed responsibility, but they cannot shoulder the burden alone. Perhaps the cruelest dimension of this tragedy is that three children who had no control over their parents’ decisions, disagreements or relationship must now live with the consequences. A mother is gone. A father is gone. Three children remain, carrying grief, medical challenges and questions that may never have satisfactory answers. They did not choose the home into which they were born. They did not choose the circumstances that shaped their childhood. And they certainly did not choose to become orphans. Yet, they must now find the strength to survive, heal, remain healthy and dream again. For them, the tragedy is not over. It has only entered another chapter—one in which society must decide whether to look away or extend a helping hand. items.title: Pakistan-sponsored resolution on self-determination adopted by consensus at UN
items.description: UNITED NATIONS: The UN General Assembly’s Third Committee on Thursday adopted by consensus a Pakistan-sponsored resolution reaffirming the right to self-determination of peoples living under colonialism, foreign domination and alien occupation, with 62 countries co-sponsoring the initiative. The resolution, titled “Universal Realisation of the Right of Peoples to Self-Determination”, was introduced by Pakistan’s Permanent Representative to the United Nations, Ambassador Syed Haider Shah. Pakistan has been sponsoring the resolution since 1981. “The promise of self-determination remains unfulfilled for many peoples still living under foreign occupation,” Ambassador Shah said, drawing attention to the continuing denial of this right to the people of Palestine and Indian-occupied Jammu and Kashmir . He said that in several situations, the legitimate aspirations of occupied peoples continued to be met with military oppression, excessive use of force, extrajudicial killings, arbitrary detentions, enforced disappearances, restrictions on fundamental freedoms and attempts at demographic engineering. Such practices, he said, constituted grave violations of international law, undermined the credibility of the international legal order and challenged the principles of justice and human dignity. Ambassador Shah noted that the exercise of self-determination had transformed the course of history, enabling millions to free themselves from foreign subjugation and establish sovereign states. The vast majority of UN member states, he observed, had themselves achieved independence through the exercise of this inalienable right. He said the right to self-determination was a cornerstone of the UN Charter and firmly established in Article 1(2) of the Charter, Common Article 1 of the International Covenants on Civil and Political Rights and Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, as well as the Declaration on Principles of International Law and General Assembly Resolution 1514. The ambassador said the resolution reaffirmed the universality and indivisibility of the right to self-determination, expressed solidarity with peoples deprived of their fundamental rights and freedoms and underscored the international community’s collective responsibility to uphold this principle. He said the resolution’s consistent cross-regional support reflected its enduring relevance to situations involving foreign occupation and alien domination. Ambassador Shah thanked the 62 countries that co-sponsored the resolution and urged other member states to join the initiative. The adoption by consensus, without a vote, reflected broad support among UN member states for the principle of self-determination.

items.title: Nigeria, Russia move to ease trade, strengthen customs cooperation
items.description: By Providence Ayanfeoluwa The Nigeria Customs Service, NCS and Federal Customs Service of Russia have signed a cooperation agreement aimed at strengthening bilateral trade facilitation, intelligence sharing and customs enforcement, while exploring mutual recognition of their Authorised Economic Operator, AEO programmes. The service in a statement said the Agreement on Cooperation and Mutual Assistance in Customs Matters, CMAA provides a framework for collaboration in customs procedures, information exchange, financial integrity, border security and personnel capacity development. Speaking, Comptroller-General of Customs, Adewale Adeniyi, who led the Nigerian delegation, described the agreement as a strategic instrument for safeguarding economic integrity, securing supply chains and strengthening trade governance. He explained that the signing followed months of technical consultations, legal reviews and constructive engagements between both administrations. Adeniyi explained that the NCS had accelerated its digital transformation through the adoption of electronic systems for customs declarations, payments and submission of supporting documents. According to him, the reforms demonstrate that revenue generation and trade facilitation can complement each other, in line with the World Customs Organisation’s SAFE Framework of Standards. On the implementation of the agreement, the Customs boss identified cooperation between the two countries’ AEO programmes as a major priority. He said both administrations would exchange experiences on their respective frameworks and operational procedures, with the long-term objective of achieving mutual recognition to facilitate the movement of cargo and reward compliant traders. The two sides also explored arrangements for exchanging customs statistics and trade data to improve analysis of bilateral trade flows. Adeniyi disclosed that Nigeria was participating in the World Customs Organisation’s data initiative. Russia’s Head of Customs, Valery Pikalyov, explained that his administration was authorised to collect and exchange customs statistics derived from declarations. Pikalyov expressed readiness to explore a dedicated data-sharing arrangement with Nigeria. The agreement also provides for cooperation against customs offences, illicit financial flows, grey-market importations, tax evasion, counterfeit goods, narcotics and other prohibited or hazardous materials. It further establishes a framework for direct operational assistance, personnel training and the exchange of professional expertise between the two administrations. items.title: Dollar to Naira exchange rate today, November 20, 2026
items.description: The Nigerian naira continued to face downward pressure against the United States dollar across both the official Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market (NFEM) and the parallel market on Friday, November 20, 2026, driven by tightening foreign exchange supply and rising end-of-year seasonal demand. Official Market Performance Real-time interbank spot tracking at the Nigerian Foreign Exchange Market placed the US dollar at ₦1,352.54 during early morning trading on Friday, following an opening rate of ₦1,351.86 and an intraday peak of ₦1,355.31. This early session trading follows Thursday’s official Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) volume-weighted benchmark, which saw the naira depreciate to a four-month low. According to official CBN data for the November 19 trading session, the NFEM weighted average rate settled at ₦1,376.58 per dollar, while the indicative closing rate rose to ₦1,388.00 per dollar from ₦1,379.99 recorded on Wednesday. Intraday interbank transactions on Thursday were conducted between a low of ₦1,370.00 and a high of ₦1,397.00 per dollar. Despite the depreciation, market liquidity improved significantly, with NFEM interbank turnover surging by 59.13 percent to $800.31 million across 184 deals, up from $502.88 million the previous day. Parallel Market Rates In the parallel market, commonly referred to as the black market, the local currency weakened further as Bureau de Change (BDC) operators and street dealers in Lagos and Abuja quoted the US dollar at a selling rate of up to ₦1,468 per dollar on Friday morning, following Thursday’s close between ₦1,461 and ₦1,468. Buying rates among informal currency dealers hovered between ₦1,445 and ₦1,458 depending on transaction volume and location. With Thursday’s official closing benchmark at ₦1,388.00 and parallel market quotations reaching ₦1,468.00, the spread between the official and unofficial windows widened to ₦80.00 per dollar, compared to ₦70.01 recorded earlier in the week. Market Drivers and Reserve Outlook Since the end of October, when the naira closed at ₦1,346.00 in the official window and ₦1,373.00 in the parallel market, the currency has lost ₦42.00 and ₦95.00 in the respective segments. Meanwhile, Nigeria’s gross external reserves stood at $54.71 billion as of November 18, 2026, reflecting a moderation of $554 million from the October 27 peak of $55.26 billion. Financial analysts note that the recent divergence between both windows is largely fueled by heightened festive import demand, corporate obligations, and reduced autonomous foreign exchange inflows rather than a structural depletion of the country’s external reserves. items.title: Why we pulled down Umeh’s billboard — Anambra govt
items.description: The Anambra State Government has dismissed claims that a billboard belonging to Senator Victor Umeh was pulled down because it carried the image of former Governor Peter Obi, calling the allegation false and misleading. The government said the enforcement action stemmed from an alleged violation of the Anambra State Signage Act, 2010, rather than the identity or political affiliation of anyone featured on the billboard. In a statement issued yesterday, the Commissioner for Information and Value Reformation, Dr Law Mefor, said that although Senator Umeh had paid the required signage fee, Peter Obi had not complied with the payment requirement. Mefor alleged that the senator, instead of fully complying with the law, used the billboard to promote the presidential candidate of the New Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), thereby contravening the state’s signage regulations. He stressed that the removal was carried out strictly in accordance with the law, which he noted was enacted during Peter Obi’s administration as governor of Anambra State. “For the avoidance of doubt, the billboard was not pulled down because of Peter Obi’s image,” the commissioner stated. The government further warned that any combined billboard campaign featuring candidates who had not fulfilled their signage obligations would face similar enforcement, regardless of their political party, status, or affiliation. It maintained that the state’s outdoor advertising regulations would be guided by fairness, transparency, and even-handed application of the law. Mefor urged the public to disregard what he described as a misleading narrative surrounding the incident, insisting that the government remained committed to due process and equal treatment in enforcing existing laws. items.title: World Children’s Day: Turning economic gains into progress for every child
items.description: Every World Children’s Day, November 20 th , gives us an opportunity to celebrate Ghana’s children and ask a simple but important question: Are we giving every child the best possible chance to succeed? When it comes to children’s rights, Ghana has much to be proud of. In 1990, Ghana became the first country in the world to ratify the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which would become the most widely ratified human rights treaty in history. Since then, successive governments, communities, and partners have translated that commitment into real progress. More mothers and children have access to essential health services, under-five mortality has fallen by more than 70 per cent, school participation has expanded, and Ghana has strengthened its laws, policies, and social and child protection systems. In recent years, Ghana has also made remarkable strides in restoring macroeconomic stability. Inflation has fallen significantly, economic growth has strengthened, and confidence in the economy has improved. As Ghana consolidates these gains, there is an important opportunity to ensure that economic recovery translates into better outcomes for every child. Yet not all children benefit equally from these achievements. Today, a child’s chances of surviving, learning, and thriving still depend heavily on where they are born and their circumstances. Under-five mortality ranges from about 20 deaths per 1,000 live births in Greater Accra to 72 in the Oti Region. Learning outcomes also remain a concern, with 45 per cent of children not achieving basic numeracy and 32 per cent not achieving basic literacy by Primary 4. Protection challenges persist, as 94 per cent of children experience violent discipline, 28 per cent are engaged in child labour, and one in six girls marries before age 18. Even birth registration varies widely, from 58 per cent in Oti to nearly 92 per cent in Western North. Ghana’s challenge is not only to sustain national gains but also to ensure they reach every child. The encouraging news is that these gaps can be reduced through smart, targeted investments that reach children at the right time and in the right place. It is important to look carefully at who benefits from public spending across categories, socioeconomic status, and location. Public spending should reflect children’s evolving needs as they grow. Yet children aged 0-5 receive only about 10.9 per cent of total public spending on children, despite this being the most critical period for brain development, nutrition, health, protection, and future learning. While investment is needed throughout childhood, a more balanced allocation would better reflect different needs at different stages. Infants require maternal and newborn care, nutrition, immunisation, responsive caregiving, and protection; young children need health services, nutrition, safe water and sanitation, protection, and early learning opportunities; school-age children need quality education, nutritious diets, safe environments, and social protection; while adolescents need access to education, health and sexual and reproductive health services, protection from violence, skills development, digital safety, and pathways to productive livelihoods. Across all stages, children need supportive family and community environments that enable them to survive, thrive, and reach their full potential. Children from poorer households continue to face greater barriers to accessing essential services. Children in the wealthiest households receive nearly twice the per capita public investment of those in the poorest, while disparities between rural and urban areas persist. Availability of services alone is not enough when transport costs, distance to facilities, gaps in school feeding, medicine shortages, or limited frontline social welfare capacity prevent children from accessing them. Public resources should increasingly be directed to the districts and communities with the greatest needs, particularly children living in poverty, children with disabilities, and those in hard-to-reach areas. As Ghana prepares to implement its 2027 Budget and Economic Policy, this principle is more relevant than ever. Fiscal prudence and investment in children are not competing priorities. They are mutually reinforcing objectives that support sustainable growth and long-term prosperity. The 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy reflects this reality. Spending in core social sectors is projected to increase from GH¢84.5 billion in 2026 to GH¢103.7 billion in 2027, representing about 26.6 per cent of the budget. At the same time, interest payments on debt are projected at nearly GH¢61 billion, underscoring how debt servicing continues to limit resources available for investments that directly improve children’s lives. Sustaining progress in debt management will be critical to creating more fiscal space for health, nutrition, education, social protection, water, sanitation and hygiene, and child protection. Education remains the largest social sector, with its allocation increasing from GH¢49.1 billion in 2026 to GH¢52.9 billion in 2027. However, improving learning outcomes will require sustained attention not only to access but also to quality. Building on the momentum generated by last week’s launch of the Ghana Foundational Learning Agenda 2026-2030, this starts with ensuring that every child has access to a qualified teacher and learning materials. Today, rural schools face particularly acute shortages, with approximately 67 pupils for every qualified teacher, compared with a national average of 37. Nutrition is equally fundamental to Ghana’s human capital. Investing in maternal and child nutrition, breastfeeding, nutritious diets, and essential micronutrient interventions helps children grow, learn, and reach their full potential. Yet despite nutrition delivering some of the highest returns on investment in children, Ghana still lacks a clear picture of how much is invested in nutrition. Better tracking of nutrition financing is essential to ensure resources match the scale of the challenge. Addressing malnutrition also requires action beyond the health sector, including improving access to affordable nutritious foods, social protection, healthier food environments, and water, sanitation and hygiene. The health sector allocation, including the National Health Insurance Scheme and the Ghana Medical Trust Fund (Mahama Cares), is projected to rise to GH¢47.4 billion in 2027 from GH¢34.1 billion in 2026. Yet access must be matched by quality. Adequate financing and improved efficiency of the National Health Insurance Scheme and primary health care services remain essential to ensure that mothers, newborns, and children receive the care they need. This is particularly important as Ghana assumes greater responsibility for financing essential services for children. The introduction of a dedicated vaccine budget line under the Ministry of Health budget is a major milestone and demonstrates the Government’s commitment to sustainable domestic financing for immunisation under the Health Sovereignty and Accra Reset Agendas. However, the allocation of GH¢100 million remains significantly below the estimated financing requirement of US$54 million needed to sustain the immunisation programme, particularly as Ghana enters the accelerated transition phase from Gavi support, with full government financing responsibility expected by January 2030. Domestic financing should also include allocations for cold chain, distribution, outreach and demand generation to ensure that vaccines purchased reach every child, especially those in underserved communities. Closing this gap will help protect Ghana’s hard-won gains in child survival and ensure that every child remains protected from vaccine-preventable diseases. Equally important are investments in water, sanitation and hygiene. Children cannot learn effectively without safe water and sanitation, and health facilities cannot provide quality care without reliable water, sanitation and hygiene services. Yet 41 per cent of schools lack basic water services, 41 per cent lack basic sanitation, 35 per cent of health facilities lack basic water services, and 46 per cent have inadequate handwashing facilities. Investing in water, sanitation and hygiene in schools, health facilities, and communities is one of the most cost-effective ways to improve children’s health, learning, and dignity while building resilience to increasing climate-related shocks. Social protection remains a vital investment in reducing child poverty. Programmes such as the Livelihood Empowerment Against Poverty (LEAP) have strengthened household resilience, with 226,000 households graduating from extreme poverty in 2026. However, the proposed 2027 allocation of GH¢1.1 billion may be insufficient to sustain current coverage, preserve the real value of benefits, and support planned expansion, with estimates suggesting a financing gap of at least GH¢500 million. Addressing this gap would help support the planned expansion to 470,000 households and strengthen poverty-reduction outcomes. Productive inclusion programmes such as the Complementary Livelihood and Assets Support Scheme (CLASS) also merit greater investment, helping adolescent girls, women, and youth build sustainable livelihoods through skills training, entrepreneurship support, and access to finance. Protecting children from violence, abuse, neglect, exploitation, and harmful practices remains an urgent priority given their lasting impact on health, learning, and future productivity. While the 2027 Budget increases funding for child-focused services, including the Domestic Violence Fund and Child and Human Trafficking Fund , strengthening child protection should complement, not compete with, social protection. Income support helps reduce family vulnerability, while well-resourced protection services are essential to prevent violence, identify children at risk, and provide timely support. Greater investment is also needed in frontline social services. Ghana currently has only 41 per cent of the social welfare workforce required nationally, limiting support for vulnerable children and families. Adequate staffing, backed by predictable operational financing, is essential to ensure effective prevention, case management, and child protection services nationwide. Ultimately, the challenge is not only to spend more, but to spend better. For every cedi invested in children, we should ask: Is it reaching the children who need it most? Is it reaching them early enough? Is it delivering quality services? And is it improving children’s lives? Investing in children is not simply social spending; it is an investment in Ghana’s human capital and economic future. Healthy, educated, and protected children become the workers, entrepreneurs, and leaders on whom the country’s future prosperity depends. In 1990, Ghana showed the world what leadership for children looks like. This World Children’s Day, we have an opportunity to renew that leadership. Let us invest earlier, because childhood does not wait. Let us invest smarter, because every cedi must deliver results. Let us invest more equitably, because no child’s future should be determined by where they are born or by the circumstances of their family. As fiscal space expands, continued investment in children will remain essential to sustaining Ghana’s long-term development and prosperity. The right investment, for the right child, in the right place, at the right time: that is how Ghana can turn economic gains into human progress and ensure that every child has the opportunity not only to survive, but to thrive. – By Andy Brooks, Representative, UNICEF Ghana
